maintopic: BOX CARS, QUOTAS AND MARKETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member was good enough to give notice of his question. Deliveries of wheat by producers to date this present crop year are well ahead of the same period a year ago. Up to June 14 wheat deliveries amounted to 248 million bushels against 218 million bushels in the same period a year ago. Deliveries of all grains are 12 million bushels ahead of the comparable period of the last crop year. As at June 15, all points have a 3-bushel delivery quota or better. One hundred and six points are at 3 bushels, 538 at 4 bushels, 509 at 5 bushels, 741 at 6 bushels and 168 at 7 bushels.
The Canadian wheat board is endeavouring to achieve as great a degree of equality as possible before the end of the current crop year. At the same time, the board must give preference to those grades and kinds of grain which have been sold for export or for which there is active demand. I might mention that exports of wheat and flour from August 1, 1955, to June 6, 1956, are 244 million bushels as against 215 million in the same period a year ago, an increase of 29 million bushels. Although later official figures are not yet available, I would think that as of today Canada has exported as much wheat and flour this crop year as during the whole of the crop year 1954-55.
There has been particularly heavy demand for grades of wheat No. 4 northern and lower and for malting barley. This has been one of the reasons for the differences in quotas at country points. I am hopeful, however, that before the end of the crop year most of the lower quota points will have been raised substantially. Certainly that will be the aim of the Canadian wheat board, the transport controller and the railways.
I may say that in my years of association with the wheat business I have never seen wheat moving at the rate that it is moving today. We have ocean boats waiting at all ports. Churchill will be opening shortly for a record movement already booked. Loadings in the country are running around 2,200 cars a day, and from now until the end of the crop year every effort will be directed toward levelling up the deliveries at country points. It may not be possible to do that completely. Points where there is a predominance of No. 3 northern grade are difficult to handle because No. 3 northern is the one grade that is not moving freely into export. Nevertheless, we will endeavour to find a place for that No. 3 northern so that deliveries can be brought up to correspond with those at points that have a free movement.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the house rose last night I had just given a very short report from the estimates committee, and in the course of that I had said that early in the discussions of the estimates committee there had been a good deal said about the matters of professional and technical manpower. Since those are questions that come under a number of items, not only in my estimates but in others, I undertook before the estimates committee to provide at a later date some information on those topics. With your permission, sir, I would like to do so now.
I want first to speak about some of the steps we have been taking with regard to professional manpower and later with respect to other types of skilled workers and technicians who are non-professionals.
Although the training of manpower is essentially an educational matter and hence is the responsibility of provincial governments, the federal government is actively concerned with our resources of skilled manpower because they are vital to Canada's whole future economic development, and also because there is a need for national studies and analyses which are of value to the whole country.
Among the Department of Labour's activities directly related to professional manpower in Canada are: one, the provision of some financial aid to those at universities; two, continuing assistance to professional workers in finding employment and to employers in securing professional workers; three, the provision of information about careers in many
Supply-Labour
professional fields; and, four, regular studies of requirements for and supplies of professional workers, and the accumulation of a wide range of detailed information about professional manpower resources in Canada.
First of all, financial aid: Financial assistance to university students has taken two forms. The Canadian vocational training agreements with the provinces provide for sharing with the provinces on a fifty-fifty basis expenditures on bursaries to worthy and needy students at universities.
The second type of financial assistance to people studying at universities takes the form of grants made for specific research purposes. For several years, my department has been stimulating research in the universities on important labour problems by making financial grants to senior graduate students and staff members.
Second, placement of professional workers: The executive and professional division of the national employment service has the day-to-day responsibility of helping professional workers find suitable jobs and of assisting employers to secure the kind of people required for professional work. In addition to bringing together workers and employers in the same locality, these activities include scouring the country for certain types of professional people in scarce supply and, in some cases, recruiting such workers overseas. The national employment service also makes special efforts each year to help university graduates find continuing employment and to help undergraduate students secure jobs during the summer months.
Third, guidance information: The Department of Labour provides information to help youth make a wise career choice, and which also assists guidance and counselling people. This information includes both monographs and filmstrips on many professional and other occupations.
Fourth, requirements for professional manpower: Every two years, the economics and research branch, in co-operation with the executive and professional division of the national employment service, surveys the major employers of professional people to find out their requirements for such workers during the next three years, and to obtain other information about the demand for these workers. The 1956 survey, which has been enlarged to cover provincial and federal government agencies and universities, is at present under way.
A longer run forecast of requirements has to be based on a general assessment of the growth of the Canadian economy. Such an assessment is now being made by the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects

Supply-Labour
and, as was mentioned by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) the other day, the Department of Labour is preparing for this commission a study of Canada's resources of professional and skilled manpower and the long-run outlook for them.
In connection with the study of professional manpower, one of the most important activities of the department is that of maintaining in a systematic way detailed information on such items as education, experience and occupations, of the majority of Canada's engineers and scientists. Similar information is being maintained on doctors and other key health personnel by the Department of National Health and Welfare.
These data are the only comprehensive sources in Canada of information on the characteristics of our manpower resources in natural science, engineering and health personnel. It should be pointed out that this information is obtained on a voluntary basis. Not everyone replies to the inquiries made, although a high proportion does so. Under conditions of emergency, such information would be highly valuable and could be extended as needed very quickly.
I should mention that there exists also information about the number of people being trained each year in various professional fields. The dominion bureau of statistics publishes data on university enrolments and graduations each year by professional field, while the Department of Citizenship and Immigration provides figures on the immigration of professional workers. There also is information on the number of professional workers emigrating to the United States, and this is by far the largest part of all emigration from Canada.
I have referred to various sources of information about our professional manpower resources. We are regularly using this information as a basis for analyses and studies. Most of this material is published in a quarterly technical personnel bulletin prepared in the economics and research branch. Over recent years this bulletin has contained special studies of the important engineering
groups, physicists and mathematicians, geologists, and of the employment experience of several of the recent science and engineering graduating classes.
The Department of Labour recently convened an advisory committee on professional manpower to serve as a medium for the exchange of ideas and opinions about scientific and other professional manpower in Canada, and to act as a consultative body to assist the department in its work in this field. Representatives on the committee came from a number of professional associations, and from government departments and agencies interested in professional manpower problems.
I do not want to leave the impression with you that we know all the answers about professional manpower. Some of my earlier remarks have indicated we do not. What we are trying to do is to use our resources in the department in ways that will pay the greatest dividends towards increasing our knowledge about Canada's resources or professional manpower. There are many problems which should be examined, and this is being done.
I have here a number of tables and charts, not very long, which give statistics. Perhaps I might outline them and thereafter ask for permission to have them printed in connection with my statement. They are as follows. Table No. 1 shows immigration to Canada in professional occupations during recent years. Table No. 2 shows the new supplies of professional persons from that immigration and from graduations over the past four years. Table No. 3 gives the same for engineers. Chart No. 1 is on the new supply of professional personnel from 1946 to 1953. Chart No. 2 is on the growth in selected professional occupations from 1931 to 1951. Finally, chart No. 3 gives a comparison of the degree of shortage and graduations of engineers from 1947 to 1955.

(Mr. Gregg.]

What I have been talking about so far has been related in the main to Canada's professional manpower. I would now like to make some comment about a broad study of Canada's requirements for non-professional skilled tradesmen and technicians in relation to future supplies. Apart from the importance of professional workers, adequate supplies of skilled and technical manpower are fundamental to the healthy development of a dynamic and progressive economy such as ours.
The productivity of industry and our competitive position in world trade depend very heavily on the skills of our labour force and on their adaptability in the light of changing technological requirements. In addition, over the next decade, many more young Canadians will be coming forward for training than has been the case over the past decade, owing to the rapidly rising birth rates of the early forties. It is also possible that Canada will not be as successful in securing skilled immigrant workers over the next few years as we have been in recent years.
All these reasons strongly suggest that increasing emphasis should be placed on the training of skilled tradesmen and technicians if our resources of skilled manpower are to meet the technological challenge of today's world. A program of research had been developed to throw light on these problems with a view to providing reliable information to assist management, labour, government agencies and educational authorities in reviewing and assessing the policies and actions which might best be taken in this important field.
Present and future skilled manpower training needs have been under consideration at recent meetings of the national vocational training advisory council. At its last meeting, the council requested that a study of this kind be undertaken as soon as possible by the federal Department of Labour in cooperation with the appropriate provincial departments and other interested agencies. This request was subsequently endorsed very strongly by the national apprenticeship advisory committee.
This research program will, of course, be centred on vocational and technical training as distinct from general education. It is recognized, however, that technical training must be built on the basis of a sound general education.
This research program might be described in terms of a three-pronged attack on the problem of vocational and technical training. The first part of the program is a project designed to evaluate industrial requirements
Supply-Labour
for skilled and technical workers as they are being affected by the rapidly changing technology of industry in several important industrial groups.
As we are all aware, the pace of technological development is being stepped up very rapidly in this country and other industrial nations and, for this reason, its effect on training requirements for skilled and technical workers will become of increasing importance. Through interviews with key personnel in selected industrial plants, associations and unions and in other ways, an examination will be made of the relationship between technological change and requirements for skilled workers. Highly competent engineers on the staff of two of our leading universities are assisting in this part of the research program.
The second phase of the program is designed to secure information on typical ways in which skilled workers acquire their competence. This is important in assessing the adequacy of present methods of acquiring skills. In this phase of the work, experienced social scientists from university staffs are assisting in interviewing electronic technicians, tool and die makers and other selected occupational groups.
The third phase of the research program is designed to evaluate our existing resources, for training skilled workers and technicians: in public institutions, in private trade schools, and in industry. This will involve a review of physical facilities, staff resources, enrolments and graduations, the content of typical vocational courses and plans for future expansion.
When put together with the information from the other two projects, it will help in making an assessment of the adequacy of our training facilities in the light of future requirements and future technological developments.
This part of the project is being undertaken in co-operation with the appropriate provincial departments involved, with industries, unions and other groups having responsibilities for the training of skilled workers.
I am sure that hon. members will appreciate that this sort of study cannot be completed quickly. We hope, however, as the facts come in, that we shall be able to put together a picture of our resources for vocational training in Canada and a picture of the probable requirements for skilled and technical workers. This will enable governments, industries and other groups having responsibilities in the training field to evaluate their training programs in the light of changing conditions.

know that, particularly in the civil service, there is a setup which is admirable and by which each person reports to a superior. I very much fear that, in the event of a breakdown in those communications, the persons who are charged with the local responsibility of maintaining order and of providing for maintenance of services will find that they will run into a stumbling block with regard to the procurement of the assistance which they need and which could be provided through the local offices.
Mr. Chairman, I think there is just one more point that I wish to raise on this first item, and that is the matter of a complete overhaul of the labour code. This is not a new point. I have spoken about it before. It is now several years since we were told in committee that this was being proceeded with. The rapid change in our working conditions and the changes which we face in the years immediately ahead of us have contributed in part to the outmoding or outdating of much of our present labour code. In fact, I do not think I would be guilty of any exaggeration at all if I were to say that the conciliation procedures and so on are antiquated. I know that in a department which has operated smoothly for a great many years there is likely to be a tendency to shy away from change, particularly overall change. There is a great tendency to feel that everything is quite all right as it is because nothing very serious has happened. But, Mr. Chairman, the time to make sure that nothing happens is in the comparative calm and quiet of times of industrial peace.
I suggest that we have had our danger signs. One of these was the necessity which the government felt it was faced with-with which we did not agree-of imposing compulsory arbitration on the railways five or six years ago. That action has had its reflection on negotiations with railway employees ever since. I must say that it is my opinion that the successful conclusion of the recent negotiations was due in large measure to the excellent services which were rendered by the chairman. I might point out that that chairman is a highly qualified person who has had startling success in that field, and that he is not a member of the judiciary.
Despite the very casual way in which the minister has brushed off the suggestion that some of the existing unions may run into difficulties over their certification, I feel that it may very well happen that the minister will be faced with a whole rash of judicial actions which will prove without doubt that the board actually has no power to recognize a bargaining unit where the name has been

changed. I greatly fear that result. I know the minister has repeatedly said that all is well and that this will not happen. I feel that this is one more place in which action should be taken immediately in order to make sure that these certifications will stand up.
With reference to the conciliation procedures which are currently in operation, may I say that I do not think there is any member of this house who does not recognize the fact that in many instances they are so prolonged that, instead of providing a cooling off period-as was said in the brief of the Trades and Labour Congress and the Canadian Congress of Labour to the Gordon commission- they frequently provide a heated-up situation which does little to help solve the dispute that is under consideration. Then, too, in those long periods of conciliation proceedings there arises at the time of settlement the grievous question of retroactivity of terms, and quite properly so because it is a fact that the worker feels that his advantage should extend back to the time when the contract was up for renegotiation. It is also difficult for the employer to make his concessions back to that date because in the meantime he has been carrying on business or supplying services under the old terms. Hence here you have a conflict of interests where you might say that both sides have a real point. Yet the whole matter could have been solved by a speeding up of the conciliation proceedings. I think that one thing that is needed is more effective conciliation board services. I must say that in some ways I agree with the brief to the commission which I previously mentioned, where it is pointed out that probably the best manner of accomplishing this would be to appoint qualified and highly paid officers who would be able to move immediately into the field and effect a settlement in the manner in which Mr. Taylor did just recently.
But I do not think these things can be done offhand. I believe the minister should take immediate steps to set up a select committee to investigate the position in which contracting parties find themselves today. I believe this committee should be composed of representatives from all those bodies who will be affected. There should be representatives from the labour congress, such representatives from management as may be appointed by their respective organizations, legal representatives, and such others as may be named by the minister, who have had long and successful experience in this field. In the last 50 years much has happened in this country in the field of labour negotiations. It is well to remember that where at one

time a member of a labour union was considered to be one step above a criminal, today he is a highly respected member of his community.
A survey conducted by the economic research branch on January 1 of this year showed that in Canada today there are, it is estimated, 1,346,000 persons who are members of unions. That is too many people, Mr. Chairman, to brush off lightly. It is true that where a man is a recognized, responsible citizen in his community, who takes part in civic affairs and who is recognized by his employer as a valuable and conscientious worker, that man, as someone has said in a brief which I read recently, though I cannot remember which one, does not change overnight into an irresponsible individual. If he is goaded into actions which may appear to others in the country as irresponsible, then I think it would be well to examine why he was forced into that position.
I have seen a man whom I respected very highly, whom I had known for many years, whose word had been taken by his neighbours and his associates in church work and civic affairs as well as other fields of activities, who suddenly was placed in the position of being a striker because of conditions which he and his fellows found completely foreign to them. This man then found himself, along with others, criticized publicly in the press and by speakers as an irresponsible individual. I saw quite a number of men in that situation just a few years ago. When I read these remarks recently which I have just described, they struck home. It is true that people do not change their characteristics overnight. If they are responsible members of the community they do not suddenly become irresponsible because they feel that they must take action which may be deemed by others to be violent. In this particular case there was no violence at all involved. It was a very peaceful strike.
Now, Mr. Chairman, for all of these reasons I feel that action must be taken by the minister's department to bring up to date the provisions of the labour code, and in particular those provisions dealing with conciliation procedure. I ask him to take another look at it. I ask him to listen to the advice which I am sure must have been given to him by responsible members of the labour congress. If he has been led to believe in the past that what was good enough for people 15 or 20 years ago is good enough for people today, then I suggest he take another look and consider this matter very seriously. I ask that we have no more delay in actually coming to grips with a complete revision of the code. We have seen no evidence at all that anything has been done, despite the fact 67509-322

that almost yearly we have been told it was under consideration. I have other things I should like to bring up, Mr. Chairman, but I think I will be content to deal with them when the appropriate items come before us.

Mr. Chairman, the question posed by the minister in his statement is one with which I am not going to deal at length. The hon. member for Hamilton West stressed that question of the shortage of engineers. I would advise any member of this house who thinks there is a shortage of engineers to take a look at the St. Lawrence seaway project. Most of the development of that project is on the Canadian side. I was there last Wednesday and took a look at it from Iroquois falls down to the Lachine canal. This project was mapped out and is being constructed by Canadian engineers. It certainly dispels the illusion that has been created over the years that we have to go to the United States for know-how because I think there is a much better job being done on the Canadian side by Canadian engineers than is being done on the other side. They are doing something on our side and that is pouring cement in the winter time which apparently they cannot do on the other side as yet.

I am not going to deal with the national labour code. I was a member of the committee that set up the code. I know its limiting factors. I think one of them is the enforcement of the code. I have argued a good many times in the house and I introduced a bill into this house that was designed to take the enforcement of the code, in the matter of certification, violations, penalties and fines, out of the hands of the courts of the country. Labour relations do not belong in the criminal courts of Canada. The department has a lot of trained personnel. Just as the government enforces the Income Tax

Act, the motor vehicles act and so on, a competent national labour board should function and the enforcement of the code should be in the hands of the labour board and not in the hands of the judiciary of this country. That is one of the things that are badly needed. I believe that if they were enforcing their code, handling the thing themselves, ultimately the limiting factors in the code today would disappear because I think they are largely matters of administration.
Then, there is the other point made by the hon. member for Hamilton West to the effect that in the event of an emergency the national employment offices should occupy the position of directors of safety in the different areas across Canada. That, of course, would mean that you would have to have national emergency powers. It was not popular in some sections of the house when we were arguing to retain it to meet the very things the hon. member for Hamilton West fears.
I was glad the minister decided to lay over any discussion of the Unemployment Insurance Act until he and his officials have had an opportunity of further studying the matter and making up their minds as to what might be done with respect to amendments, and then taking it back to the industrial relations committee, the committee which worked on the amendments to the act last year, for the purpose of further discussing it and finally bringing it back to the house and handling the matter here when there is nothing else in the way. That was a good decision. As a member of the committee I appreciate the fact that hon. members co-operated with the minister to the extent they have on this particular point.
There are many spots in the minister's department that we could be critical of, and we must be, but this department is doing a lot of good that is not generally known. I do not think the sending of the estimates to the estimates committee shortens the time or serves very much purpose except that it gives the members who are on the committee an opportunity to get a lot of information that they would not get were the estimates taken up in the house cold. I know the briefing we got in the committee from the minister's officials was valuable in so far as the members of the committee were concerned, and, of course, it is our job to pass on to the members of the house any information we receive.
There is one spot that I was rather critical of, and I still am, and that is the movement of workers in Canada from province to province. There are spots in this country where we have permanent unemployment which necessitates the movement of workers from
[Mr. Gillis.l
that area to other parts of Canada. For example, there are men going from my own area to the logging industry in British Columbia. That is a long way from home. They are going as far from home as an immigrant who comes in here from Europe. The transportation of those people to British Columbia is not assisted in any way by the government, but immigrants who come here from Europe under the department of immigration can go to a hostel in Montreal and be housed there and maintained while the immigration department goes out and finds jobs for them. If they have to move to another part of Canada they are assisted in their passage and at the same time they are guaranteed medical coverage for the first year of residence in any province of Canada while they are in the country and go out to a job. My criticism is that if we can do that-and I am not objecting to it-for immigrants, the same principle should apply in the movement of workers from Cape Breton island to Vancouver, which is taking place, or to Steep Rock, where others are being sent. I am asking the minister and his cabinet colleagues to take a look at the question of assisted transportation for workers who are moving within Canada. Never forget that many of these people are ex-service men and many of them were previously employed and were taxpayers for a long time. Unfortunately, their employment has disappeared because they were working at mining which is a wasting resource. They find that although they had an investment in the community they had to move on. The least that can be done is for the government to assist them with transportation.

As I said before, the department are doing many things which are beneficial but they are not known. Take vocational training for example. The officials of the department gave us an excellent brief on what is happening in that field. That brief was quite wide and comprehensive. It indicates that the legislation provides many opportunities for the provinces to do something with respect to training young people or retraining unemployed. I have in my hand the document with which we were supplied and it proved a real revelation to me. I try to keep track of all these things, but I did not know about much of the material in this document. It is a worth-while plan and hon. members of the committee should take a look at this kind of thing.
The minister is authorized to undertake and direct research work, to disseminate information in the field of vocational training. It is provided that the minister may enter into an agreement with a province for a given period to provide financial assistance up to an amount equal to that expended by the province. Many types of training are provided for. There is the training of supervisors in industry, rehabilitation training of disabled civilians, training to increase the skill and efficiency of workers in agriculture, forestry, mining, fishing and other primary industries, including homemaking.
The initiative in taking advantage of the legislation rests with the province. That is 67509-322J

something which is not generally known. Many people will ask what the federal government is doing in connection with vocational training and they do not understand that the initiative must be taken by the province. Agreements must be entered into. In my judgment the legislation can do a good job of work in any province provided the province is willing to co-operate.
As the minister knows, a school was set up in North Sydney during the war for rehabilitation services. It did a good job and trained a total of over 3,000 people, many of whom are scattered across this country in responsible positions. The school was allowed to run down and the equipment was practically all moved out. A couple of years ago the minister and I began to talk about the rehabilitation of that school to re-train unemployed. That was done and the school has been in operation for the last two years.
When I was home last November I visited the school and it happened that 20 students were being graduated in diesel mechanics. They have a very good setup there to train diesel mechanics, about as good as you can find anywhere in the country. They have over $200,000 worth of diesel equipment on which the boys are working under a competent instructor. Every one of those 20 young boys who were being graduated was going to a job, many of them to the C.N.R. shops, to work on diesel equipment.
The supervisor of the school is a most capable person and recently I wrote to him to ask how things were going. He tells me he has a course in diesel mechanics, sheet metal, two classes of auto body mechanics, and courses in welding, carpentry and plumbing. He is teaching six different trades. The enrolment shows that approximately 24 per cent never worked before; 33-8 per cent are receiving further training in their chosen trades, while 42-2 per cent were unemployed and are being re-trained in other trades. The school can accommodate about 200 pupils and I understand there are about 80 enrolled at the present time.
These students are learning trades which are most essential today. The brief I have here indicates that the Department of Labour is conscious of the need of training in various trades. It is indicated that there is a shortage across the country in the skills which are being taught in this little school. In my judgment vocational training and trade training in these centres is most important.
Of course every section of the country wants a vocational high school which would come under the department of education of the particular province. While trade training is carried on the entrance qualifications

are a little more difficult than in the case of the trade training centres. I hope to see a vocational high school on Cape Breton island before long, but the people I am chiefly concerned about at the moment are those who have been able to go only to the eighth or ninth grade and do not intend to go through a high school. A high percentage of boys and girls leave school after finishing the eighth, ninth or tenth grade. They are not interested in university training, either because they are mentally handicapped or because it is financially impossible for their parents to have them go any further. As I say, the department is doing an excellent job in connection with trade training, but I want to stress again that it is up to the province to take advantage of the federal legislation. The legislation is available to solve the problems which exist in that field.
There was another matter in connection with which we received a brief which was all information to me, and that is student's aid. I received many letters in this connection. A boy may finish high school and perhaps his first year in university and then find himself financially embarrassed. He wants to know where he can go to get a loan in order to finish university. I was not aware that the minister's department was able to supply an answer to that question until I sat in on this committee.
The mechanics are that a board is set up in each province which receives applications from students requiring loans. A student must be recommended either by his high school teacher or by a member of the faculty of the university to which he intends to go. But loans, grants and bursaries are available. With the legislation that exists and is being administered by the minister's department and other departments of the federal government, I do not think there is any need for any young person in this country who possesses the necessary capabilities to be denied a university education. I believe the machinery is there in the minister's department.
The first approach is to the local board in the province. I am putting all this on the record because I want this information to get out to the country where people may read and understand it and know exactly where to go. There have been many a young boy and girl who could have gone through university had they known about this legislation, but they did not. In my judgment the minister's department has the answer to getting a boy or girl through university, provided they know the proper approaches to make and the people to contact.
Another section with which I was very much impressed was the women's bureau.

For the first time in the committee we met the lady who administers the women's bureau and we were handed some literature. That bureau, in my judgment, is going to make a valuable contribution to the minister's department. The work that they are doing and the grasp that that woman has of her own particular section of the department in the short time it has been functioning were very encouraging, and, I might say, very complimentary to her. I hope that over the years that section will be built up and that more women will take part in studying labour relations, because it is a very important sector of our society, it is the wealth-producing end of our society, and women can play a very important part in it. I just want to compliment that lady for the job she is doing now in setting the mechanics for the future in that particular section of the minister's department.
Next I wish to say a few words about annuities. That, of course, is a very unpopular subject to some people outside the house. A few years ago the minister tried to amend the act and to write in a cash-surrender clause, which I think should have been written in, but with the barrage from coast to coast of pressure groups he retreated. I hope it is just a retreat and that he will organize and move forward at some time in the future. That is another branch that is not generally understood. The person who administers that department gave us a very good picture of what the annuities branch is doing, and I am going to put that on the record.
There are at present 64 full-time and 21 part-time annuity representatives located in 50 major centres from Halifax to Victoria. Overhead expenses, including the compensation of annuity representatives, are paid from general government funds. The proportion of expenditure to receipts is less than 2 per cent. That is not much to complain about.
The annuities branch consists of six divisions and is located in No. 5 temporary building, Carling avenue. These divisions are: group, actuarial, individual contracts, accounts, sales and administrative services and legal. There is a staff of 174. This is a reduction of 38 since 1949-50, even though there has been an increase in the volume of work. Contracts and certificates under administration are 100,000 more in number than in 1949-50, and there are 30,000 more cheques being sent out each month.
As of March 31, 1955, there were in force and under administration by the annuities branch 159,532 individual contracts and 190,129 certificates under 966 group contracts, a total of 349,661 contracts and certificates; payment of annuity is being made under

68,130 of these contracts and certificates. The annuities fund as at the end of March 1955 was $864,543,038, and the net receipts for the year were $68,594,250.
I just thought I would put those statistics on the record for the information of those who scream from time to time: "You should not be subsidizing these annuities." Well, there is not much of a subsidy, but the important thing to remember about the annuity is that it has been a yardstick for the insurance companies across this country over the years. It has at least kept them looking at their rates.
Another point I wish to make is this. The group insurance contracts that exist in industry all over this country are based on the actuarial work done in the annuities branch. Industry does not have the facilities to do that. That branch has done a very important job in setting those group contracts, and they are still farming them out.
I wanted to say that and to put those few statistics on the record, but I hope the minister will get around to writing in that cash surrender in the annuity. Mistakes have been made in taking in people, for example, veterans and civic employees. I am thinking of my own end of the country now. Many veterans established contracts under the annuities branch, and these veterans were taken in under protest. They said, "We do not have to go in; we have the protection of the War Veterans' Allowance Act." But they went in, and after one or two years the department finally permitted their release. They were released, but the money is still there for the two years when they paid in, and they cannot get it back under the present contract or under the present act. Many of these are young men who have since married and are building homes. They have a few hundred dollars that they would like to get out to use for building homes. I believe that is merely an administrative matter. I think that even under the present act, where there are extenuating circumstances such as that, the minister and the administrator of the act might be able to sit down and release the money that was tied up and that belongs to people who did not want to go in in the first place but were taken in by the town or city as the case might be. That is found right across the country, but it is a pertinent question in my own end of the country.
I notice that my time is just about to expire. Like the hon. member for Hamilton West, there are odds and ends that I have not dealt with yet, and I shall have to deal with them under the appropriate items.

The minister is administering a very large department. We will have to vote altogether in the neighbourhood of $70 million to $75 million for his department this year. We know that labour plays a tremendously big part in the nation's business. It seems to me that the particular function of the minister's department is to see that labour and industry run as smoothly as possible and to make regulations here and regulations there in order to get out of labour and industry the very best that they can give to this nation's welfare.
1 do not place myself in any position of severe criticism of the minister or his department. I will say, however, that generally speaking I think that industry and labour in Canada will run smoothly enough while industry is able to expand, while we have a time of comparatively full employment. I wonder though what may happen should the eventuality arise where industry ceases to expand. What then? Suppose industry ceases to expand by reason of a recession or depression. We do not like those words. We hold up our hands in holy horror as we think of that possibility but we must not put on the ostrich act and put our heads in the sand.
We here are not only responsible for the things that happen today. We are responsible tor the things that may happen in the years to come, and we must legislate and discuss legislation on the basis of what is going to happen tomorrow. I do not look for any immediate depression. I am not going to appraise the future but I do believe that if a recession or depression should happen and industry fails to expand the country is going to be plunged into chaos.
My hon. friends who have preceded me have discussed the lack of engineers. I too do not know what the statistics are but I believe we have good reason to say that there

speechtext:
I am not talking about engineers or any particular profession. I am saying that everything is nice and rosy, everything goes along lovely as long as the country is going through a period of expansion, but as soon as that expansion ceases we are plunged into depression and chaos, and even the strong labour movements we have in our country cannot cope with that sort of situation. I would proffer this thought to the minister, whether he will agree with it or not. The labour movement have fought over the years for the position in which they find themselves today. That is well and good and I do not want them to lapse into any inferior position having regard to the position they are in today. In days of prosperity even the labour movements become stronger, if I might put it that way, and are able to accomplish for the working people of this country the thing that they are after; but as soon as depression comes, even labour movements begin to break at the seams and fall apart. That is something that I think even organized labour itself should take into account, and I think it should prepare itself for that possible eventuality.
Unless we get down to the basic and fundamental principles of our whole industrial system we are not going to solve what eventually might be a terrible problem that this country would have to face. I think that labour and management and government perhaps at all levels should take a new look at those basic principles which make our entire industrial system function. Several questions must be asked. There is no use in dealing with secondary things. If there is something basically wrong, you will not heal that basic ill by fooling around with secondary things that may appear to be wrong. We must ask ourselves some questions such as these: What is the purpose of industry anyway? Is the purpose of industry to give people jobs? As I have said before in this house, I say that the purpose of industry is to produce goods and services. I am not going to debate the pipe line but that, to my mind, is an advance in this country's expansion. If I had my way, we would have many pipe lines. If I had my way, we would have many trans-Canada highways. There is a great deal that we can do provided that the purpose of these things is recognized and provided that the basic principles are made to apply in order that we may serve that ultimate purpose.
What is the purpose of industry? Is it to give people jobs? We assert it is not. We assert that the purpose of industry is to produce goods and services that can be distributed to the people so that they can have a
Supply-Labour
higher standard of living. What is the purpose of production? Is the purpose of production to give people jobs? No; the purpose of production is to produce in order that the nation may consume. What is the purpose of labour? Is it to make money? Is it to make a fast buck? Is it to increase salaries? The purpose of labour, of course, is so to fit into industry that they are able to produce the goods. That is the purpose of a job. But of course we have lapsed into a complex where we have become so money-conscious that we think the purpose of a job is to get money; that the purpose of industry is to get money; that the purpose of everything in the country is to get that dollar which is so hard to get. We might go a little bit further and we might say, "What do we want to get the dollar for?" That is the thing. We want to get the dollar because we believe it will buy something. What do we want to buy something for? Because in the ultimate conclusion the things that make for life and happiness are the things that we produce.
We have said over and over again that we are living under a dog-eat-dog system and that is why, in a system that is basically wrong, one class is pitted against another. A man once said to me, "If you do not beat this system, the system is going to beat you". So what do you have? You have a scrap. I do not like to refer to dogs because I might get into trouble by referring to them. However, the system works like six hungry dogs fighting over five bones. What is basically wrong? There is no use saying, "We will have to produce better dogs that are able to fight a little bit better" or "We will have to produce better bones". There is no use in talking along that line. We assert that is exactly what is wrong with the system. So all we say is, "That should be easily remedied; throw in an extra bone so that there are six bones for six dogs". But no; that is not the government policy.

maintopic: NEW SUPPLY OF PROFESSIONAL PERSONNEL, CANADA, 1946 TO 1955
speechtext:
I should like to say a few
words this afternoon about part of the estimates that come under the minister concerning education. Some time earlier in the session I had the pleasure of introducing a resolution dealing with aid for needy university students, and I should like to take this opportunity of thanking all those in the different parts of the house who supported me that day. Today I want to speak more specifically about technical and scientific assistance.
I am not unmindful of the assistance that the federal government has already given in this sphere. For example, we all know that this year, 1955-56, the federal government has decided to give some $7-8 millions in unconditional grants to the universities in Canada. We also know that vocational training assistance in 1954 by the federal government amounted to $1,350,000. As I mentioned previously on another occasion, the house is also aware of the fact that student aid has been granted to students who wish to attend universities and who would not otherwise be able to attend because they have not the financial means.
I might say, Mr. Chairman, that a very good example of the lack of assistance was brought home to me once when I was coming to Ottawa one Sunday afternoon on the train. At that time there were some students from the collegiate institute at Oshawa who wanted to attend university next year. But upon questioning them I found that they did not have the means. Presumably they were both above average from an academic standpoint or they would not have been chosen to represent their schools at the Rotary convocation here in Ottawa. Neither one of these students knew where they were going to get the

money. Apparently they had not heard about student aid. I think possibly that has not been publicized sufficiently, and I say that with respect. I think the government, in co-operation with the provincial departments of education, is doing an excellent job.
In dealing with this matter of education, of course, it is necessary to reiterate time and time again that education generally comes under the jurisdiction of, and within, the ambit of the different provincial governments. In other words, the British North America Act gives general education exclusively to the provinces and it is most important that the federal government do not impinge upon this general constitutional right. But, Mr. Chairman, there are certain specific fields in which the federal government can give assistance without impinging upon this jurisdiction, and that is one thing I should like to talk about this afternoon, namely vocational, technical and scientific aid. I would hope that the federal department of labour would endeavour to assist in this field to a greater extent. I think we all in this house appreciate the sympathetic consideration and the very great administrative ability the Minister of Labour has brought forward in this field. I for one, and I think most members of the house would agree, feel that once the fiscal arrangements have been developed between the provinces and the federal government this aid could be greatly extended. I think we would all welcome that time.
It is rather interesting that in this house today the question of the need for scientific personnel was brought up. In an editorial in last night's Toronto Star there was one paragraph that I should like to quote to the house. The Star was discussing the conscription issue raised by a Canadian general. I am not going to discuss that, Mr. Chairman, but I do want to quote this one paragraph, which I think is relevant. The Star said:
What Canada desperately needs Is more engineers, technicians, doctors, school teachers and other qualified professional people. The federal funds which General Simonds would spend on compulsory military service would be better employed helping Canadian educational institutions turn out graduates required for the development of this country- and the health and progress of its people.
I am quoting that because I think that that is the general opinion in this country, that we do need more trained personnel. I think it is important to trace the historical background of the development of our country if this basic premise is correct, and I submit it is. Canada has changed in the last 50 years from a predominantly agricultural economy to one which is concerned with the processing of raw materials and the development of products of the mines

and the forests. In other words, it has been changing from an agricultural economy to a manufacturing economy with the tertiary industry of service. We have been changing our whole economy in this country, and of course agriculture in itself is becoming more specialized. It follows from that, Mr. Chairman, that we will be needing an increasing number of specialists in Canada. I am informed that in 1931 there were 420 engineering and science graduates; in 1952 there were 1,770; and in 1958, it is estimated, there will be 2,250. I am interested in the observation of my hon. friend from Brandon-Souris in which he claimed that 1,500 more engineers could receive positions if they were graduated this year. This seems to me to be reasonable and I would think that that conclusion would be correct, although I have no statistics to back it up.
It is interesting to compare those figures with the figures for the United States. In the 20 years from 1930 to 1950 there was an increase in United States engineers from
260.000	to 850,000, a growth rate of 227 per cent, whereas in the same period the population in the United States increased only 23 per cent. It is estimated that in Canada in 1975 there will be 16 million people over 14 years of age, and the non-farm labour force will be 7,500,000 as compared with the
4.600.000	now. We can, therefore, expect our requirements for professional workers to increase by more than 60 per cent over the next 20 years. Another reason for the increase in technical and scientific personnel will be seen in the growth of the country, the gross national output it might be called. In 1949 the gross national expenditure was about $16 billion; in 1955 it is estimated the gross national expenditure will exceed $21 billion. If one were to project this to 1975 it is estimated it would be $48 billion.
Again, we have the matter of technological changes. We all know what a tremendous impact on our country's growth the introduction of atomic energy has made. We are all aware of the vast and far-reaching effects of automation. New professions have come into being, such as town planning. For example, in my constituency of York Centre, where there is a tremendous housing and industrial development, town planning is very important, as is traffic control. Indeed when one picks up the Sunday edition of the New York Times one can see the demand for such specialized activities as designers of business machines; instrument engineers, semi-conductor engineers, telephone engineers, guided missile engineers, nuclear engineers, structures engineers, transistor applications specialists, and so on.
Supply-Labour
It is a very bewildering world, Mr. Chairman, and I submit it is going to become increasingly so the more science is advanced and the more technical knowledge is ascertained. Now, of course, the government does help out in this field. I have already mentioned vocational training. I think hon. members are aware of the scholarships of the national research council and the defence research board.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, a very important reason why we should train more technical men, more engineers and more scientists can be found in the struggle, shall I say, between the soviet orbit and the western world. The influential and authoritative British weekly, New Statesman and Nation, pointed out on Saturday, January 21, that there will be 4 million technical graduates turned out by the Soviet union in the next five years. As a matter of fact, Dr. Solandt, formerly chairman of the defence research board, now vicepresident of the Canadian National Railways, put it this way in the fall of 1955:
The present relative stability of the world depends upon a balance of defensive and offensive capabilities between east and west. This balance in turn depends upon the productivity of scientists and engineers in the two halves of the world. Since 1950 it has become increasingly obvious that, at least in certain selected lines of development, the Russians were actually overtaking the west. Recent attempts to find the explanation for this phenomenon suggest that it lies in the field of education. Because of this the output of scientists and engineers in the U.S.S.R. has overtaken and passed that of the U.S. and may soon exceed that of the major nations of the free world combined. The best evidence we have suggests that this increase in numbers has been achieved without any sacrifice in quality.
And now, Mr. Chairman, this statement shows more conclusively than anything else that unless we have an increase in the number of scientists and technicians in Canada and in the western world we may well lose the battle to totalitarianism in this field. Of course, I have not said anything about the humanities. It is interesting to note that the president of Du Pont of Canada Limited, I believe, was reported in the Montreal Gazette of yesterday morning as saying that it was a mistake to emphasize the engineering aspect too much; that we should also emphasize the humanities. I hope that nothing I have said today will be construed as implying that I wish to weigh the balance against the humanities. Probably it is desirable to stress the fact that in this world at the present time we need more engineers and more technicians, but we must not neglect the humanities, we must not neglect the arts. My plea would be for increased assistance both to scientists and to engineers and to those who are pursuing the humanities.

Supply-Labour
Just before one o'clock I heard one of my friends state that engineers might well be a glut on the market if a depression were to occur. Mr. Chairman, I think we on this side of the house and in this country have indicated that we certainly do not expect any return to the 1930's. The fact that more and more economists are being trained who are making specific studies into business cycles and the fluctuations in world economic conditions is one of the best reasons why we should continue to turn out more trained men. Actually, education is not a burden to anyone. The more university graduates that are turned out in the sciences, in the humanities, in the social sciences and in economics, the more opportunity we in the nation will have to prevent cyclical depressions, cyclical recessions, and so on. Therefore, that is one good reason why we should turn out more engineer graduates, more university graduates all the time.

Mr. Chairman, more than five years ago, in response to considerable public pressure for a rehabilitation program to meet the needs of disabled persons across the country, this government set up an advisory committee known as the national advisory committee on rehabilitation to study the whole question and bring in recommendations on which the government might hope to base a program. That was five years ago, Mr. Chairman. We have heard nothing, literally nothing, of any plans the government now has, after those five years, of introducing a rehabilitation program aimed at meeting the rehabilitation needs of disabled civilians in this country. It makes you believe that this was just another government committee, like the manpower committee and so many other committees that this government sets up when it is faced with a problem with which it has no intention of grappling. They simply make a big hurrah, set up a committee, and then completely forget about the whole issue. I would like to see some indication from the minister, if what I am saying is not correct, but there is no indication to the contrary so 
far, and it appears that the government intends simply to let the matter of rehabilitation die.
We have an order in council, known as the co-ordination of rehabilitation agreements order, under which the federal government is willing to share with the provinces in the co-ordination of rehabilitation services, provided that those services do not cost more than $15,000. Mr. Chairman, you cannot go very far in a program of this kind with $15,000. Therefore, that order in council will not get us very far.
Then, we have schedule R of the Canadian Vocational Training Co-ordination Act, which is administered by the Minister of Labour, and under which the federal government is willing to share equally with the provinces in a vocational training program. Useful though that is, it is only one small part of a rehabilitation program. So far there is no provision whatsoever for the federal government sharing with the provinces in the cost, first of all, of medical and surgical rehabilitation; second, the provision of artificial limbs; third, vocational guidance; and fourth, social services. Those are all very important components of a rehabilitation program.
One of the great weaknesses in this whole matter is that rehabilitation falls between two ministers, the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of Labour, with all the resultant confusion and lack of co-ordination that one would expect from such a dual responsibility. I do not think we will get anywhere in connection with rehabilitation until this matter is placed under one minister or the other, and until the government spells out what services are to be provided for, or purchased on behalf of, disabled persons and for which the federal government is willing to share the cost with the province. Until that is done, the provinces will simply not be able to know where they stand in regard to the division of cost with the federal government, and quite frankly, they are not prepared to go ahead on their own until they do find out.
There is no reason why rehabilitation services should not be provided in this country for disabled persons in exactly the same way as rehabilitation services have been provided for our veterans and as they have been provided in certain provinces for civilians who fall into certain definite categories. For instance, in the province of Ontario, excellent rehabilitation services are provided by the Ontario compensation board for accident victims, and the rehabilitation program provided by the Canadian National Institute for the Blind for blind people right across this country is well known to all.

What is the attitude of the United States government toward rehabilitation? It is both enthusiastic and progressive, and is at complete variance with the lackadaisical attitude which this government adopts toward this important problem. The United States government is engaged in a program to increase the number of disabled civilians who will be rehabilitated each year, from 60,000 last year to 200,000 in 1959. This is an imaginative, progressive and comprehensive program, which is at great variance wtih the attitude of this government toward this problem.
The United States government has found that rehabilitation pays off in dollars and cents. In addition to the greatly improved health, morale and usefulness of the disabled person, the United States government has calculated that during the lifetime of a rehabilitated person, $10 is returned to the federal treasury in income taxes for every $1 which the government pays out for rehabilitation services.
What is the situation in Canada today? So far rehabilitation services are provided only for special categories such as disabled veterans, industrial accident victims in certain provinces, the blind and paraplegics. A great majority of the disabled civilians in this country cannot obtain rehabilitation services.
In order to establish a comprehensive rehabilitation program for which all disabled civilians would be eligible as of right, financial participation by the federal and provincial governments and voluntary agencies would be required. Money properly administered for the purposes of rehabilitation is the one thing needed to initiate such a program.
I am advised by those who have studied this problem closely that what is needed is the introduction of a Canadian disabled persons rehabilitation act, which would provide money for the provincial governments and voluntary agencies on a shareable, grant-inaid basis, for the purpose of establishing adequate rehabilitation programs in the provinces and subject only to necessary administrative safeguards. I believe all hon. members of this house would gladly join in approving such legislation because I believe everyone is convinced of the rightness of the principle that all disabled persons should have the opportunity to lead normal and useful lives, and that this right should be regarded as a fundamental right of citizenship. For that reason I urge strongly once again that this government bring forward such legislation at the earliest possible opportunity.

Mr. Chairman, I have a rather sad but proud duty to perform on
Supply-Labour
behalf of our late colleague, Dr. Jack Mac-Dougall, the late member for Vancouver-Burrard. As many hon. members know, for some months before his death he was very much concerned with one problem and I had been in consultation with Dr. Mac-Dougall, and with Mr. Tip O'Neill, the former member of parliament for Kamloops, about the matter which I am now going to raise. Jack MacDougall had told me that he intended to raise it at this time and I had promised to support him in his submission. The matter concerns a rather considerable number of superannuated employees of the Canadian Pacific Railway whose pensions have amounted to less than $60 per month. They are, of course, a minority of such superannuated employees.
I am sorry that I cannot give the exact number of such pensioners, but there is a goodly number all across Canada and their organizations, especially the Pacific coast C.P.R. pension association of 1953, had specifically requested the late Dr. MacDougall to raise this matter on the floor of the house at this time because they thought that by his so doing it would focus the attention of the Canadian public on this matter.
The crux of their grievance, which was embodied in a brief originally submitted in the year 1953, is that in January, 1953 the basis of the C.P.R. pension system was changed in two important respects; first, to increase the pensions the deductions from wages were raised from 1 per cent to 1J per cent and, secondly, future pensions are to be calculated either on the last five years of service or the last ten years of service, whichever gives the best results to the pensioner. The basis of the complaint was that those who had retired before 1953 had no way to benefit on a par with those who retired later although their living expenses had gone up the same as those of everybody else. Therefore the Pacific coast C.P.R. pension association made the following three specific requests:
1.	That the basic pension be not less than $75 per month to those under 70 years of age, and not less than $60 per month to those over 70.
2.	That the so-called single life plan be made
applicable to all-to apply to wives of men who retired prior to January 1,	1953, where their
husbands at that time elected to take the single life plan; and
3.	That all employees who had retired to January 1, 1953, be given the benefit of the 1| per cent computed on their present pension.
After considering the matter and hearing the representations of the men the management of the Canadian Pacific granted quite substantial increases as from February 1 of the present year. While expressing deep satisfaction at these increases the Canadian

Supply-Labour
Pacific pioneers' pension committee made the following submission in a letter to the management of the company dated April 12, 1956: Dear Sirs:
The pension committee, on behalf of those pensioners who retired prior to January 1, 1953, wish to express our appreciation and thanks for the revised changes in the pension rule, effective February 1, 1956.
These new rules will bring some relief to those specifically affected up to 70 years of age.
We find, according to statistics of ages of pensioners from the auditors' report, that the increase to $60 per month for those below 70 years of age, while of great benefit to those below that age, apply to few in number, which number is steadily decreasing, and would not seriously affect the solvency of the pension fund if continued after the age of 70 years.
Later in the letter, which is signed by Mr. A. S. Emms, chairman of the Canadian Pacific pioneers' pension committee, it is pointed out that the cost of living is still increasing and that many of the pensioners find it difficult to eke out a respectable existence.
I know that a narrow interpretation of our rules might hold that such matters should not be raised in this house on this vote. However, I would submit that the C.P.R. is an institution of which the whole of Canada is deservedly proud, and also, because of the existence of its great competitor, the C.N.R.- which is owned by the people of Canada-that any question concerning the equity of the pension fund of either or both railways is a matter of legitimate concern to every member of this house.
In any event, I feel it is a great honour to have the privilege of raising on the floor of this house a matter about which our late colleague, Dr. Jack MacDougall, had had so much correspondence with the railway pensioners.
On earlier occasions, I have had the privilege of supporting the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in his exhortations for justice for some of the C.N.R. pensioners- especially those former war veterans who are really in a pitiable condition, some of them drawing as little as $25 per month.
In this case I want to pay tribute to the C.P.R. for having made the limited improvements which they have made, but to urge with all my strength that they comply with the reasonable request of the C.P.R. Pioneer Pensioners' Association.
