This matter of aid to university students has come before the house in the labour estimates today. However, during the last two or three months important organizations and institutions have been talking in the press about the need of training more students, especially in science, and the need for more engineers. I was rather surprised

this morning when the hon. member for Cape Breton South said he felt that the universities were in the business of training scientific students for the sake of training them and that there was a profit motive in this matter. I was also surprised that the hon. member for Macleod spoke about depressions and the fact that it was not certain that we needed students trained in this country. When the hon. member for Hamilton West spoke about the matter of training university students, I am sure that she was talking about the shortage of these students in connection with planning for the future.
In so far as students are concerned, I have had some correspondence regarding the difficulties of science students in earning their own way through college. I am perfectly aware that the income tax as such must have some rigid lines and must apply, but in the case of students over 21 years of age I am going to submit part of the letter written to me by a boy concerning this matter. It is true that there is a $1,000 deductible clause. In one case the boy is over 21, and that is the time when they are in the third or fourth year of science, and he is putting himself through college. They are usually healthy young people at that time. He has no other deductions, such as for sickness; he is not making any charitable donations; and so it all rests on that $1,000 deduction. I know this boy's people. They are a very fine family and they have already educated three sons. They are contributing a great deal to this country. This boy puts it in this way:
Dad paid $70 income tax for me on that summer's earnings, which was equivalent to the government taking away 70 per cent of the $100 scholarship I received that year.
That boy won a $100 prize for efficiency in some of the scientific subjects in that year, which was his third year. He goes on:
The average year at Queen's (engineering) costs $1,200; therefore, in order to put himself through a student would have to earn $1,800 in the summer; of which $400 would go for board and lodging for the five summer months away from home; income tax would take $160; leaving him $1,240 for his university year.
I hope that the Minister of Labour will talk to the Minister of Finance about this matter and that something will be done. If these boys are going to try to put themselves through university, there should be some relief in so far as income tax is concerned. It seems rather hard that they should try to educate themselves and at the same time pay income tax when it would be only a small matter, in so far as the government is concerned, for a student earning his own way through college, particularly in the engineering subjects, to be relieved of the necessity

of paying income tax. It seems rather hard that they should pay income tax and then not have enough money for their university year.
This has been recognized before, and I am going to quote from a speech of one of the Liberal members in the provincial legislature concerning this matter. This was Mr. J. J. Wintermeyer, newly-elected Liberal member for Waterloo North. He considered this of such importance that he made it the subject of his maiden speech in the Ontario legislature. He said that Ontario and Canada are lagging far behind other countries in producing university graduates and that this loss would soon seriously cripple the provincial and national economy unless immediate steps were taken to remedy it. He said that the problem was difficult, but the rewards to be gained by having more skilled university students would give Canada a wealth that would not be estimated in dollars. He went on to point out that in England 70 per cent of all university students were receiving government financial aid of some type.
Further to the question of the criticism that was made this morning of the universities, I want to bring before the house the position of these students. Many of the universities a few months ago announced increases in the costs of the university course. I am referring to the costs of the course of the University of Toronto. These increases are the third that have been announced since the end of the 1950-51 academic year. The annual fee for a general arts course was then $242; it will now be $335. That is in the faculty of arts, but one must agree that the course in science is much more expensive, and that is what we are particularly dealing with today. Applied science and engineering fees have risen from $347 in 1951 to the new level of $500-at a time when the shortage of engineers is impairing our development in this country. It is hindering not only our development at home but also the Colombo plan projects abroad.
With regard to what the hon. member for Cape Breton South said concerning this subject, let me point out that, despite these increases, tuition fees have been providing an ever smaller proportion of total university expenses. In the current year, they make up only 26-7 per cent cent of the University of Toronto's revenue. Thus, scholarships, which merely cover tuition fees, are costing the university more and more all the time.
With your permission, sir, I wish to read into the record on this subject statements made by Mr. James S. Duncan, C.M.G. We all remember that series of articles that Mr. Duncan wrote when he came back from Russia. My repeating some of the statements
Supply-Labour
of Mr. Duncan's does not mean that I approve of the present form of government in Russia in any way, but we are in competition, both in peace and in war, with that country-or in cold war-and Mr. Duncan says something in his report that deserves recognition. This is the twelfth article in the series and these articles were carried in newspapers throughout the country. I am certain that Mr. Duncan is a well known man who knows what he is talking about, and that the review he made of educational conditions in Russia, especially with regard to training scientists, can be accepted in this house by any person. In this article he points out;
There are over 30 universities in Russia, and many hundreds of colleges and institutions of higher training, including technical and polytechnic institutes. Although it is difficult to obtain reliable figures, I am informed that Russia turned out nearly twice as many graduate engineers last year as the United States did, and that their engineering training is not only as good as ours, but when they have completed their five and a half year university course, they have put in 50 per cent more study hours than our students.
I shall go on and read some other extracts from this article regarding the aid that is given in that country to train students in science. Some of this is rather amazing. Mr. Duncan says:
Each student receives a monthly allowance from the government which, when the merit bonus is added to It, is sufficient to cover his fees and living expenses. In the first year the student's allowance is 290 rubles ($72) per month and is just about enough to exist on. In the senior courses the allowance is increased to 500 rubles ($125) monthly.
I am only reading parts of Mr. Duncan's report. He says that all reading and textbooks are supplied free. Then he has this to say:
Out of their allowance, the students pay 400 rubles ($100) per annum for their tuition, 30 rubles ($7.50) per month for their rooms-
Then he goes on to point out that they are served meals in the canteens at a very low rate. But this is the important thing so far as we are concerned. Mr. Duncan says:
There is also a concerted drive in Russia to produce mathematicians, chemists, physicists and other scientists, and these are being turned out in rapidly increasing numbers.
I started by making an appeal for help to university students. Having in mind the small amount that it would cost the government, I ask the consideration of the Minister of Finance, and to the Minister of Labour may I say that he could use his good offices in bringing this matter before the Minister of Finance, so that university students who are trying to earn their own way will not be penalized by having to pay income tax and having to borrow money or have somebody

Supply-Labour
help them to pay their income tax in order that they can proceed with their university courses.
I leave this matter before the minister. I think there is something wrong when such a condition exists. Certainly we need more students in this country, and in spite of what has been said by the hon. member for Macleod with regard to the possibility of a depression, I still have faith in Canada, whatever the political complexion of the country may be. I think of a statement I made in the house two or three years ago when something like this came up. Political considerations might enter into this question but I think of a statement by an American, quite a philosopher, who, in dealing with the question whether a democratic or a republican government would do more for the United States, said, "This country is too big to be destroyed by any political party".
Canada will grow. We have natural resources and we do need engineers for the development of our country. Therefore I think every possible assistance should be given to these people in order that they may qualify and aid in the building of our country. That is all I wish to say on this matter. I again make the appeal that every assistance be offered to university students and that in cases where they are earning their own living it would be a small matter to relieve them of income tax.
There is one further question I want to bring before the Minister of Labour. It has to do with my own riding where a large industry moved away and left a lot of people unemployed. As a result skilled tradesmen, toolmakers, people of that type, men who had been employed in the industry for years, find it difficult to obtain another job. The situation has reached the point, and I think the Minister of Labour should take notice of it, that if a man is 40 years old or more it is practically impossible for him to get a job. Industries nowadays are looking for people who will fit into their pension plans. When a man who has been employed as a crane man applies for a similar job in another industry he is politely shuffled aside if he is 40 years old or more and is told that there is no place for him. If that were the situation, then there are many of us in the House of Commons who should not be here.
I maintain there is a place in industry for men from 40 to 65 years of age. From the point of view of experience alone they have a great deal to contribute. Put yourself in the position of a man 40, 45, 50, 55 or 60 going out and trying to obtain another job and being told very politely and nicely by the employment officer, "We have got nothing 
for you today." What is at the bottom of the whole problem is that industry does not want to employ men 40 years of age or more because they do not fit in with their pension plans or the so-called routine of the particular industry.
I think the Minister of Labour might well look into the matter, especially with regard to the industry to which I referred which was in a town in my own riding. There are a lot of very fine people there. Their unemployment insurance payments ran out on the first of May. They are qualified craftsmen but when they go to look for another position there is no place for them. Many of them are excellent citizens who own their own homes. If they sell their homes it is going to be the beginning of a drop in real estate prices. If they move to another area, an area where employment is easier to obtain, a booming area, they are going to pay a great deal more for their homes.
There they are in that position. Their unemployment insurance ran out on the first of May. The minister may say that other jobs are open. If a man 40 years or over is unemployed does it simply mean, so far as the unemployment insurance people are concerned, that he has to go and take a job as a road labourer or something like that? Other industries will not take him on, and so he is in a most difficult position. I feel sorry for these people. They are the best people in the world and yet they are in that position. Nothing is coming in. I repeat once more that their unemployment insurance ran out on the first of May and when they go to get another job they are too old because they are 40 or over.
I bring these two matters before the minister today, the question of consideration for university students and the matter of looking into the situation of people who are 40 years old or over. It may seem ridiculous when I say 40 years old but firms are not hiring them in spite of the fact that they are skilled tradesmen. In the situation they are in they need income at the present time and in view of the fact that they are unemployable and cannot get a job because of their age something should be done for them and every consideration should be given to their position.

Mr. Chairman, first of all r should like to indicate my unqualified support of the plea made a few minutes ago by the member for Vancouver South. In doing so, I am registering the support which the late member for Vancouver-Burrard knew would be registered by a number of us when the time came that he would have made the plea that has been made in his stead today

by the hon. member for Vancouver South. Indeed, I am satisfied that there are other members, members in all parties in the house, who will support the plea that has been made in the hope that even yet the Canadian Pacific Railway will give favourable consideration to the points that have been drawn to the attention of that company by organizations representing their retired employees.
Since the member for Vancouver South has put most of the details on the record, it is not necessary for any of the rest of us to repeat those details, but may I just say that it seems to me that the most serious aspect of the matter, the point over which there is the deepest feeling of grievance, has to do with the cut-off date of January 1, 1953. As the hon. member for Vancouver South has already pointed out, both in his own remarks and by reading some of the correspondence, the new pension rules of the Canadian Pacific Railway came into effect on February 1, 1956. In so far as any greater contributions that have to be paid by those still working for the Canadian Pacific Railway are concerned, those greater contributions are effective only from that date, namely February 1, 1956. Yet it is a fact that any who were in the employ of the company after January 1, 1953, even though they may have retired prior to February 1, 1956, or if they retire now, get the benefit of the new rules. Those benefits are in the main two in number: on the one hand an increased pension for the worker himself, and on the other hand a greater pension for his widow if the retired worker dies first. The other side of the picture therefore is that with respect to employees whose retirement date was earlier than January 1, 1953, they do not get either of these benefits. They do not get a greater pension as of right nor is there the greater protection for the widow when the employee dies first.
My contacts with these people, like the contacts of my hon. friend across the way and the many contacts that the late Jack MacDougall had, I think will bear out this statement, namely that although these men are naturally concerned and disappointed in that they do not get the greater amount of pension to which they feel they are entitled, what worries them most is the realization that if they die first the position of their widows will be an extremely difficult one.
It has to be recognized that this is not a matter concerning which the parliament of Canada normally legislates and I suppose in a sense it might be said that it is not a matter upon which parliament would be expected to legislate. But it is true that there are relationhips between the government of
Supply-Labour
Canada and a great corporation like the Canadian Pacific Railway, and I would feel that it is part of the responsibility of the government, in view of its desire to maintain good labour relations, to offer some good advice to the Canadian Pacific Railway in a matter of this kind. I also believe that if views on this subject are expressed by a number of members representing all parties in the house, the Canadian Pacific Railway might take our views into consideration.
To argue-as the railway does on an occasion such as this-that the matter is one of a contractual relationship, it seems to me does not meet the point; for the fact is that there are employees most of whose contributions were made previous to the change in the rules-in other words, when the contributions were at a lower rate-who nevertheless get the benefit of the higher pension both for the employee and for the widow. As I say, that applies to those who retired after January 1, 1953. There are instances of men retiring in December 1952 and in January 1953. The difference in the total amount of money paid into the pension fund by employees retiring in those two different months is practically nothing. Yet the difference in the pension earned by the employee can be $50 or $60 a month and the difference in the pension that would be paid to the widow can be of the order of $25 or $30 a month or more. As the hon. member for Vancouver South has indicated, there is a considerable file of correspondence, documents and memoranda on this subject. A number of us in the house have copies of it. From my study of it I feel that the C.P.R. has been most unfair towards employees who happened to retire just before January 1, 1953, and I hope that the company will reconsider that matter.
I say again that there are other jurisdictions that have increased the pensions of those already retired. I regret that is not true of the federal government with respect to its superannuated civil servants. I regret that it is not true with respect to the Canadian National Railways. But it is true in the case of at least three provincial governments in this country; it is true on the part of the government of the United Kingdom, on the part of the government of the United States and on the part of the governments of a number of states. I also know that there are some private corporations in Canada that have increased the pension not only of those still working for them who retire in the current period but of those who retired even in years gone by. I repeat another instance of which I have personal knowledge, namely that of the International Typographical Union to which I happen to belong which has been increasing its pension across the years.

Supply-Labour
In fact, the pension that is now paid to retired members of the union is twice what it was 10 years ago. May I emphasize the fact that persons who retired 10 or even 20 years ago, or at any time in the past, whose contributions into the fund were on the former lower rates, get the benefit of the increase in pension without having to pay any more into the fund. I regard a plan of that kind as human, fair and just and I see no reason why other jurisdictions or a company like the C.P.R. should not also be human, fair and just in its dealings with its former employees.
It is obvious that this is a matter on which any of us who are briefed could speak at some length; but perhaps it would be better if, instead of two or three speaking at length, a number expressed their support of the position that was to have been taken by the late hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard but which was expressed by the hon. member for Vancouver South, so that the Canadian Pacific Railway will know that as human beings, interested in decent human relations, we think the C.P.R. should take another look at this issue.
Mr. Chairman, I should now like to say a few words more directly to the Minister of Labour with regard to what I would consider to be the tremendous opportunity he has to play an important role in the future of this country. Because it is part of his task to listen to briefs and to peruse documents that are presented to him by labour organizations and because it is part of his task to keep in touch with what is going on in labour circles, he knows that in the main the requests which labour makes to parliament and to the government fall into two categories. On the one hand labour is constantly seeking legislation for the benefit of the community as a whole. In this category there are requests for national health insurance and for social security legislation such as adequate old age pensions, improvements in family allowances, improvements in unemployment insurance and so on. There are as well many other types of things that labour requests for the good of the community as a whole. In addition to that category, labour also requests of the government and of parliament legislation concerning procedures governing the relationships between management and labour. It is in this field that labour asks for revision of the national labour code. It is in this field that labour today is still asking for consideration to be given to any amendments that might be necessary to be made to the British North America Act in order to make possible uniform labour and social legislation across Canada. It is in this field that labour asks
Mr. Knowles.]
for such things as legislation governing hours of work per week, legislation governing minimum wages, vacations with pay, statutory holidays, equal pay for equal work for women and so on.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I said a moment ago that I would like to press upon the minister, if I could, the key position that 1 think he holds with respect to the future of this country. If he will consider for a while the philosophy that underlies these requests that labour makes, and also if he will consider the new era into which imperceptibly but in a very real sense society is moving, I think he will realize the key position he holds. The philosophy that underlies these requests is, I am sure, well known to the minister and to the house. It is that labour feels that the wealth that a nation like Canada produces, whether it be the more modest volume of wealth that was produced a generation or two ago; whether it be the $27 billion or $28 billion per year that is being produced now or whether it be the much greater volume that may be produced a decade or two hence, that wealth is made possible to a very large extent by the contribution made by the working people in this country in whatever calling, whatever category, their work may fall. It is the philosophy or the approach of labour, the workers in this country, that those who make possible the production of these great volumes of wealth, should enjoy its benefits.
It has indeed been the struggle of labour across the years to get the kind of legislation, the kind of relationships between management and labour, between both of those entities and the government, that will so order our economy that as great wealth is produced it will come, not just to the few, but to all of those who participate in its production. Hence, when labour asks for national health insurance on an all inclusive basis; when labour asks for old age pensions of $60 or $65 a month at age 65 without a means test; when labour asks for the 40-hour week or for a guaranteed minimum wage of a dollar an hour; when labour asks for vacations with pay or for statutory holidays with pay; when labour asks for unemployment insurance across the board rather than unemployment insurance part way and a form of relief for the rest, labour is asking not for some handout, not for a form of charity, not for the government to play the role of Santa Claus, but labour is asking rather for what it believes to be its right. It is asking for what it has earned and is asking for its share of the wealth that labour itself has produced. That is the basic philosophy which has been underneath the requests and the demands of labour from the earliest days when labour organized in this country or in other lands.

I suggest to the minister it is becoming a philosophy and an approach that is very important in the new era into which we are moving. Living as we are in the midst of days when automation is becoming a fact, living as we are at the beginning of an era which may see a tremendous increase in the available sources of energy because of the development of atomic power, we must realize how imperceptibly but nevertheless in what a real way we are moving into a new era.
I suggest that if in the past in order to hold society together, in order to make progress, in order to make it a human society, in order to make Canada a country that was important for human beings, it was desirable for labour to make these demands and win them step by step even through a process of struggle, that it becomes even more important in the years that lie ahead that this philosophy be accepted. The government boasts of the $27 billion or $28 billion of production which may be the result in Canada this year. If we move on into the era of automation, if we move on into an era in which atomic energy is added to the other sources of power we have with the result that we have greatly increased sources of power and energy, this $28 billion we are now capable of producing may some day look like a very low figure. What is going to happen if we do double or treble the amount we are producing at the present time unless we get established this basic principle that labour has fought for, namely that all this wealth that is produced should benefit, not just a few, not just those who control it, but everybody? We could find that the progress we are making could be our undoing.
Many of the things that are implied in what I am bringing to the attention of the Minister of Labour call for legislation that falls under the direction of other ministers than the Minister of Labour. But it seems to me he is the man who should be giving to the cabinet, to the government and to parliament, a vision of what could be done because of the new era into which we are moving. I call upon the Minister of Labour not to be the tool of the government in resisting those things that labour demands, a revision of the national labour code, amendments to the British North America Act to make possible uniform legislation regarding hours of work, minimum wages, and so on. I ask him not to be the tool of resistance against vacations with pay and to give us the usual line about it being a matter for collective bargaining, or to resist statutory holidays with pay or to resist other improvements affecting equal status of women and so on. Instead of resisting that kind of thing, I call upon him to recognize that right in this
Supply-Labour
type of legislation may be the key as to whether or not these great resources that we are tapping, this great volume of production that is going to be ours in the years that lie ahead, will hang around our neck like a millstone or whether it will be the basis for an enlarged life for all the people in this country.
In the same vein I suggest it is part of the minister's job as Minister of Labour and as minister for labour, the man who should be speaking in the cabinet for the working people of this country whether they work in the factories, on the farms, in the offices, the fisheries, the mines or what have you, he should be speaking on their behalf to the other members of the cabinet and saying that this great wealth which this country is now capable of producing should result, not 35 or 50 years from now but right now, in improvements in our old age pension, in other social legislation and in the early enactment of national health insurance and other things of that kind to get back to the millions of Canadian people who produce this wealth, not a handout, not charity but that which is their right because it is labour, the working people on the farms, in the factories and offices of this country who make possible the production of this great wealth.
I say to the minister that it is not only an administrative job that he has in this important department. As others have said, he does a good job in administering the department. I suggest to him that his job is much more than that of an efficient administrator. His job should be that of a visionary, indeed I might even say a prophet. He should see what there is ahead. He should see what tremendous progress we can make if we will parallel with this era into which we are moving, the era of automation and atomic energy, the kind of legislation that will get the wealth that our people produce back to them in the form of a higher standard of living, social security, protection against ill health, old age and all these other things over which we have no control. I call upon the Minister of Labour to match the administrative job he is doing with the job of a visionary; I call upon him to urge the government to take some real, progressive steps in the direction of the kind of social legislation for which labour has been asking across the years, which labour has presented to the government very strongly, very forcibly, in the platform of principles, and the other resolutions and pronouncements that were made at the recent founding convention of the Canadian Labour Congress.
I think it is significant that just at this time, just at the beginning of this new era, when

Supply-Labour
I feel sure we are moving forward, we have this significant event of the founding of this new congress. It was a pleasure to see the minister there at least one day and the Prime Minister on another day. I hope they will read again the resolutions that were passed at that convention; that they will read the powerful speech that was made by president Claude Jodoin when the convention reached the point where the new congress had actually come into being. I call upon the government to pay more serious attention to the suggestions that have been made by that new congress which, I suggest, have underneath them a philosophy that is good for Canada, a philosophy which, if acted upon, can hold the promise of a much better day for all the people of this land.

maintopic: NEW SUPPLY OF PROFESSIONAL PERSONNEL, CANADA, 1946 TO 1955
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to deal briefly with three specific points that have been discussed here in other years, and have actually been mentioned during the discussion that has already taken place since these estimates came before us. First of all is the fact that we have been urging now for several years that the government take the necessary steps to conduct the kind of inquiry that would result in a labour code for Canada that would be a source of pride to every one of us.
It is now more than 13 years since a general examination of our labour legislation took place. Those of us who had occasion to have some contact with the results of that inquiry will recall the very satisfactory results which flowed from the report of the commission headed by the Hon. C. P. McTague which reported in 1943. At that time we were in the midst of perhaps the most severe days of the second world war, and the results of that finding were brought into effect by an order in council which did in fact provide Canada with something in the nature of a labour code covering a very wide part of our labour legislation in this country.
I strongly urge the government to take the steps without delay which will start the work either of a commission or of a committee on which there will be representation of the government itself, of the organized workers of this country, of management and of all other interested parties. We have urged this continuously since 1950. I mention 1950 because it was in 1950 that we were all called back here, those of us who were members, to deal with the situation which had resulted from the strike affecting the railways at that time. We said then that what had occurred was an illustration of the inadequacy of our conciliation methods, and that the situation with which the workers of Canada and the people of Canada generally had been con-
CMr. Knowles.]
fronted emphasized the need for a full and complete inquiry which would give to us in Canada labour legislation of the most modern and most sensible type and which would be of advantage to the workers, to management and to the people of Canada generally. The things that have happened since that time have emphasized the need for such an inquiry. Only in the past few weeks have we been relieved of the concern which was shared by all Canadians, and certainly shared by the workers employed by the railways themselves just as much as anyone else, over the possibility of a repetition of the situation with which we were confronted in 1950.
As has already been pointed out by the hon. member for Hamilton West, it is not to be suggested that people who show the very highest degree of responsibility in their daily work, such as is shown by employees of the railways, would be any less responsible in dealing with the problems of labour relations, conciliation and the general activities of organized labour.
In the interests of our workers in all activities in Canada, in the interests of management and above all in the interest of Canadians generally, I urge the minister to recognize there are many reasons now why it will be more suitable than ever before that such an inquiry take place. All of us have expressed our admiration of the way in which the Canadian Labour Congress started on its new course under the guidance of a man who commands the confidence and respect of all Canadians, whatever their occupation may be. The speech of Mr. Claude Jodoin at the time that the new congress was formed was a model of responsibility and vision in regard to the part that organized labour plays in the life of our whole country.
Now, there is the great advantage of one large responsible body speaking on behalf of the greater part of organized labour. Part of the difficulties that might have been presented by the existence of two large congresses-and in fact, I should say three large congresses-is removed in some measure by the organization which has now taken form.
The minister has on different occasions suggested that we might expect some review of this kind. I think the time is now past for speculative suggestions as to when this may be done. I think we should have an unqualified assurance from the minister that he will seek the co-operation of the appropriate representatives of organized labour, of management and of other bodies who might be brought into this inquiry, and that either a commission or a committee with full powers to inquire and report be set up for the purpose

*of considering the labour legislation of this country and recommending a labour code which will bring to organized labour, to management and to Canadians generally the advantage of the most up-to-date labour code in the world. We should not be satisfied with anything else in this country which is progressing so rapidly in every field of human endeavour.
I think one reason that we should hope this would take place is that we see the advantageous results which flowed from the last inquiry. At that time I had some measure of personal responsibility in regard to labour legislation in the province of Ontario as premier of that province. Just as soon as the new legislation, which was based upon the report of that inquiry, became law we adopted that same code and made it applicable in the province of Ontario. Later other provincial governments followed the same course and as a result we have uniform labour legislation in this country affecting a large percentage of the workers of Canada. I think if we had an inquiry which commanded the confidence of the workers, of management and of the people of Canada generally we might be well on the way toward a very extensive measure of uniform labour legislation in this country. Therefore I repeat my request to the minister that he give us assurance at this time, which we have now been seeking for so many years, that an inquiry of this nature will take place.
May I speak of another subject. This has been mentioned over and over again but it needs to be mentioned until something is done about it. This government set up a manpower committee to which it appointed representatives of various activities in this country. That committee should proceed with its work so that we may know exactly what is the situation across the whole of Canada in regard to the employment situation generally and to the need of various parts of Canada. This is not just a matter of knowing how we can use manpower, it is a case of knowing exactly where the manpower is and exactly what the situation is in regard to manpower in every part of Canada. For instance, we know that in spite of the demand for workers in many parts of Canada there are other parts of the country where there is a substantial measure of very severe unemployment.
This is the sort of thing which should be examined. With a thorough examination of "that situation the government would be in a better position to exercise such influence as it is called upon to exercise from time to time in encouraging the growth of new industries in those areas where there is need
Supply-Labour
of new opportunities for work and employment. I do not need to mention several places in this country where at this time it would be of great humane value and of great advantage to the Canadian economy generally if encouragement were given to the growth of certain types of industrial and other employment which would take up the slack which has resulted from the changing nature of some of our activities in this country. Therefore, I urge the Minister of Labour to revise the activities of this important committee and to permit and encourage it to carry out the duties which were assigned to it when it was set up a few years ago.
I want to deal with one other subject which has been mentioned in this house on different occasions, the subject of vacations with pay. I would hope that the government would take advantage of this opportunity to introduce legislation as a government measure just as it has done in other cases where the leadership has been given by the opposition. We now have before us legislation in regard to equal pay for women for equal work which is before us as a government measure directly as a result of the repeated efforts of the hon. member for Hamilton West. I would hope that we might also have for the same reason legislation brought before us as government legislation to provide vacations with pay for all those affected by the federal labour law.
Here again perhaps I may be forgiven if I speak from personal experience. It was under the government which I had the honour to head at that time in the province of Ontario that the first legislation in Canada was passed to provide statutory holidays with pay. I know how satisfactory it proved to be and I know from my own experience that not only was it of great advantage to the workers but that management also regarded the legislation as having very real and substantial advantages. Since it became a statutory obligation upon all employers to give a certain minimum number of holidays with pay there was no chance that one employer would find himself in a position of disadvantage because he followed the proper, just and humane course in providing holidays with pay on his own initiative. By the statutory provision all employers were encouraged to extend this very desirable provision, which is to the advantage of all Canadians.
The fact that workers get holidays with pay and in that way have the opportunity for recreation and the restoration of their health in itself is not only of great advantage to them and to their families, as is their just right, but it has proved to be of great advantage to the general morale of our industrial

Supply-Labour
workers who have benefited from the legislation. Therefore in view of the experience which has shown the beneficial results of legislation of this kind, and in view of the fact that we shall be sitting here for some considerable time, I hope the government will take advantage of the opportunity that is presented to introduce legislation of this nature during the present session and make applicable to the workers of Canada, at least during the latter part of the summer months of this year, the proper benefits that would flow from legislation of this nature.

maintopic: NEW SUPPLY OF PROFESSIONAL PERSONNEL, CANADA, 1946 TO 1955
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure that all hon. members have found the remarks which have been made today not only interesting but, I should think, instructive. I ask for but a few minutes of your time to deal with one subject which relates to the province of Quebec, one constituency of which I have the honour to represent. I was particularly interested in the remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for York Centre in respect to university grants, and inasmuch as the constituency of St. Lawrence-St. George has within its boundaries one of the great universities of Canada I feel this is a matter which particularly concerns my riding and myself.
Constituting as we do a minority race or group in the province of Quebec, it is sometimes said that that province leans more to the classical side and the field of the humanities rather than to the technical or scientific sides of education. This afternoon I should like to say that at least in recent years that has not been quite the fact. I believe that in the province of Quebec we will be able now to find in the field which is perhaps incorrectly called labour-because we have moved in the last 40 or 50 years a long way from the time when the man who went out with a dinner pail was just a labouring man and we are all in some degree members of the labour group-men can now be found in the trades who are as skilled as in any other part of the Dominion of Canada, though it is true that they have retained to a very large degree the basic urge for study in the field of the humanities and classical education.
Therefore when the minister is prepared to answer questions, I would like him to corroborate the information, which I believe is true, that in the last 10 or 15 years the federal parliament has granted to the province of Quebec, as it has to other provinces in Canada, substantial sums of money in capital and bursary amounts in the field of technical and scientific training. I should like him, if he has the information handy, to tell us what those amounts were, say over the past 10 years, in what particular places

in the province of Quebec they were allocated, and what use, so far as his department knows, has been made of those grants.
After all, the one person who must be served, whether we as members act in the federal field or in the provincial field or in the municipal arena, is essentially that same person, Mr. Taxpayer. When grants are made of this or that sum of money to this or that area of life, Mr. Taxpayer in the final analysis is the person who must pay the shot. I have been given to understand that substantial grants have been made to the province of Quebec and that use has been made of those grants over the past decade in this field of scientific and technical training. Therefore, when the minister replies, I should like him to put that information upon the record.

maintopic: NEW SUPPLY OF PROFESSIONAL PERSONNEL, CANADA, 1946 TO 1955
speechtext:
I was indeed glad to hear the hon. member for Vancouver South mention the problem which had been the concern of the late member for Vancouver-Burrard. I have been one of those associated with this gentleman in discussing the problems of a small group of pensioners affected in the manner mentioned by the hon. member. I am going to say nothing more than that I am pleased the matter was mentioned and will lend my support to the hon. member at any future time he wishes to bring this before the house.
In speaking on the estimates before us, I wish to say that I was a member of the committee on estimates, and when the figures for this department were before us I was impressed by the sincerity of the minister and the various officials who appeared before us and with their deep conviction that something more than was being done at the present time would have to be done in training our labour force for the future.
First I should like to refer, as has already been done in this house this afternoon, to the provisions made for rehabilitation. This is one of the newer endeavours of the department. I understand it was inaugurated in 1953. Naturally progress is going to be slow, but I understand now that all the provinces of Canada are sharing in this scheme, contributing on a 50-50 basis toward the cost of educating and rehabilitating the handicapped and the aged. We all know that many employees affected by changes brought about by machines and the automation about which we hear so much have lost their jobs and have reached the years when it is difficult to find new employment. It is for these people that there is a growing demand for training at the present time. As regards the handicapped, we are beginning to find that men and women who a few short years ago we

thought could not be used in any manner in our labour force are now being trained so they can assume a fitting place in the circles of labour, provide a livelihood for themselves and contribute to the economy of Canada.
This has a twofold benefit. Many of these people, if it were not for this special training, would possibly be a charge against the welfare contributions of this country. So, by making them self-supporting, we are probably just taking a rather selfish view that it is cheaper and of more benefit to Canada to give them this training at the expense of the taxpayers than to have them continue on the welfare rolls.
Now we have this commission set up under our Department of Labour to provide this training. Each province that agrees to cooperate with the department must set up a committee, I believe, of three members to administer the affairs in that particular province. This committee consists of a co-ordinator, a representative of the department which provides the training, and a federal representative. In my own province of British Columbia this is handled by the Department of National Health and Welfare, and I know it is performing a wonderful service for those who need this special type of training.
All applications are referred to this committee, and they are carefully screened. The aim of the committee is to find the type of training which it thinks would be best suited to the applicant, depending of course on his degree or type of disability. As I say, it is proving very effective and producing very good results, but I sometimes think possibly the people of Canada and the people of various communities are not aware of just what is available to them under this branch of our service to the people. Possibly it would be of benefit if we were to give some publicity to it.
We have heard a great deal today about professional training. The hon. member for Lanark made a very good plea and put it before the house in a very plain and straightforward manner. I am in accord with what he said. I should just like to place on the record what is being done under the plans of our Department of Labour for assisting students to get this type of training. The province of British Columbia is also taking full advantage of the scheme, which was started some ten years ago and is steadily expanding. The last complete figures are for the year 1954, and in that year the following were assisted financially in British Columbia under the joint plan of financial assistance carried on by the province and the federal Department of Labour. There were 74 students in medicine, 14 in veterinary medicine, 58 in
Supply-Labour
dentistry, 32 in pharmacy, 86 in applied science and engineering, 11 in arts and science, 174 in arts, 15 in law, 22 in teacher training,
9 in home economics, 8 in agriculture, 19 in commerce, 6 in forestry, 22 in nursing and 28 miscellaneous. This is a grand total of 517 who took advantage of the plan which is available in Canada for university training.
Looking over the total for Canada it is rather interesting to note that this is 25 per cent of the total who received training in that year. I think you will agree that the province of British Columbia and the people of British Columbia are taking full advantage of what is being offered to them. In addition to this professional training, there is much being done in promoting technical training, again under joint provincial and federal financing. Under this plan each province is given an outright grant of $10,000 for administrative expenses. During the last year for which figures are available $2,070,000 was allotted to the provinces on a per capita basis, and this per capita basis involves only the teen-agers from 15 to 19 years of age. A further sum of $10,304,950 was granted toward the cost of erecting technical schools and purchasing equipment.
So we see that the department has started along these lines; and while I would certainly agree with every member who has spoken today that there is room for much improvement and that much larger grants of money are necessary in order to give the people of Canada who wish to avail themselves of this training which is so necessary today the opportunity to do so, I believe that not even yet have we reached the point where we are taking full advantage of what is being offered. Of course until we reach that stage the government has the excuse, though it may be a poor one, that there is no use providing any more money until people are prepared to make use of it. In addition to the technical training there are also correspondence courses available, and there is also the scheme of apprenticeship training.
Today, as we approach the era of complete automation, we are certainly going to find that everyone who has not a skilled trade or profession of some kind will be absolutely at a loss in finding employment. Even today the old fashioned ditch digger has been replaced by the machine, and the idea of hand labour and unskilled labour is pretty much a thing of the past.
As has been said, we cannot force our young men and women to take advantage of these courses. However, I believe that we as members of parliament can do a lot if we will just have the problem before us at all times and, as we visit the various parts of our

Supply-Labour
ridings, give greater publicity to what is being done and what is available. At different times we may have the privilege of speaking to school classes or even service clubs, boards of trade and so on, and I am quite sure they would be glad to hear about what is available through the provincial and federal plans for better education for the people of Canada.
We know there are shortcomings in our training system, but these are being ironed out. I say with all sincerity that whenever any constructive criticism was put forward in the committee by any member I found that it got a good hearing, and we got a promise from the minister or the appropriate official that some action would be taken to rectify whatever was considered amiss. But I think if we co-operated a little more with the authorities, promoted publicity for all these schemes, and reached the stage where there were possibly more applicants than could be taken care of, we would then be in a strong position to come back to the government and say this has been started, it has proved satisfactory, but we must have more money.
I listened with interest to the hon. member for Broadview, and was rather pleased to hear his outline of what has been done in the United States. What has been done there is, of course, a target at which we may shoot. Finally, I say that the way to move any government to further action is by popular demand, and I am sure if our people make use of all the facilities offered and demand expansion, we can then get that expansion.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to offer my congratulations and sincere thanks to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) on behalf of the bushworkers of the province of Quebec, for his humane and fair attitude with regard to unemployment insurance for those people.
On February 13, 1956, the Canadian International Paper advertised for bushworkers in every employment office in the province, offering $5.00 to $6.00 per 100 cu. ft. cord of pulpwood cut in its camps. These men, who were at that time receiving unemployment insurance benefits were advised of this offer made by the C.I.P., but the vast majority of them refused on the grounds that the amount offered per cord was inadequate. They declined to go and cut wood for $5.00 or $6.00 a cord. As a result, unemployment insurance officials suspended payment of benefits to these men. Those who were members of the U.C.C. then protested against this unfair decision. They asked their federal

members to have this injustice corrected by the unemployment insurance commission. An impressive group of federal members from Quebec therefore met with the Minister of Labour to explain the situation and ask that this injustice be redressed.
After a thorough inquiry into the matter by senior officials of the unemployment insurance commission, the minister made a statement in the house on March 15, 1956, but I shall not take the time of the house to read that statement.
Following this statement the vast majority of bushworkers received their unemployment insurance benefits, and the C.I.P. remained without the extra hands needed to cut its wood. In order therefore to secure the necessary manpower on April 3, 1956 the company offered through the employment offices in the province of Quebec, $7.50 to $8.50 per 100 cu. ft. cord, i.e. an increase of $2.50 a cord.
Without the intervention of the bushworkers and of the federal members, the Quebec bushworkers would have had to cut wood at $5.00 and $6.00 a cord. It is obvious that the Canadian International Paper has once more attempted to take advantage of the bushworker by offering $5.00 and $6.00 a cord, knowing perfectly well that these prices were below the average price paid by other Quebec lumbering companies.
It is fortunate that there is a professional organization representing the farmers of Quebec and known as the Union Catholique des Cultivateurs, whose directors are men of intelligence and insight, imbued with a spirit of social justice. These are the true defenders of the rights and interests of the farmer and bushworker.
It is obvious that the Canadian International Paper is capable of paying and should pay higher wages to these bushworkers, as well as the highest prices for the pulpwood it buys from farmers or settlers, since according to the financial reports for recent years, its net profit is increasing yearly by approximately ten million dollars.
Unfortunately the Union Nationale government failed to show the same willingness or eagerness to meet the request of the members of the U.C.C. who, in their brief submitted to the hon. minister of lands and forests, on January 15 last, requested that the government set a floor price of at least $20 a cord for pulpwood bought from settlers and farmers.

In February 1955, Mr. Goulet, Liberal member for Temiscamingue in the Quebec legislature, urged the Union Nationale government to set a floor price of $20 per cord for pulpwood bought from settlers and farmers by lumber companies, but the Hon. Maurice Duplessis replied that his government could do nothing to improve the situation.
It is therefore obvious that the Union Nationale government not only fails to protect the interest of settlers and farmers but does join hands with some powerful corporations in taking advantage of workers and farmers.
Fortunately farmers today are better acquainted with such matters and they are determined to elect in Quebec a Liberal government which will know how to protect and defend their interests.

Mr. Chairman, this group believes in an appropriate scientific division of labour. Consequently I am not going to deal with a number of questions that will be dealt with by other members of this group. But before proceeding to the main purpose of my few remarks I want to express my support of the hon. member for Vancouver South and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in their plea on behalf of a certain group of C.P.R. pensioners. I know that the late Dr. MacDougall intended to deal with this question quite fully. I wholeheartedly support the plea they made on behalf of this group of people this afternoon.
I have had the opportunity to discuss this matter at length on several occasions with Mr. "Tip" O'Neill and I must say that the pensioners are extremely fortunate in having a man as active and as capable on their behalf as is Mr. O'Neill. I have seen him riding a locomotive between Kamloops and Field for a good many years, and I know him quite well. I think he has done his very best on their behalf. I also had the opportunity to discuss the problem with a group of pensioners in Nelson and a group of pensioners in Revelstoke. I have also had the opportunity to read the brief and the correspondence supplied to me by Mr. O'Neill.
I think this group of pensioners have a very sound case. I hope that Mr. O'Neill's pleas, the pleas of others and the comments of members during this debate will move the company to the action that I think the case of these worthy people warrants.
When I was dealing in another debate with the question of the recruitment of labour in
Supply-Labour
Europe to work in the mines in Canada, in reply to certain questions I had raised with respect to Mr. Ramsay's trip to Europe, the minister, as reported at page 4993 of Hansard, said this:
The purpose of his trip was primarily to secure workers for the base metal mines.
I am quite sure the minister gave the house the information he had at the time, but I am under the impression that the minister has been misinformed. I should like to direct his attention to an article that appeared on the financial page of the Toronto Daily Star of March 5, 6 or 7 last. I am not quite sure of the exact date owing to a certain amount of disorganization in my office caused by the pipe-fine debate. Anyway, in that article I found that the president of the Canadian metal mining association stated that these people were being recruited in Europe primarily for the gold mines, and that representations were being made to recruit these people in Europe to work in those mines particularly. I just draw that statement to the minister's attention because I am quite confident that he has not been correctly informed up to date.
In the few minutes in which I wish to deal with this question I want to place a few figures on record. I want to give a few figures with respect to wage rates in base metal mines and in gold mines. As to base metal mines, I know that in the Kootenay area our base metal miners get something over $2 an hour. In Sudbury they get $1.96. In Steep Rock-that is iron ore-they get $2.20 an hour. In Cobalt they get $1.51. As to the gold mines, I find as follows. I have figures for only Timmins and Kirkland Lake. At Timmins they get $1.32 an hour. At Kirkland Lake mines, I am informed, the miners get $1.29 an hour. These are the wage rates in the base metal mines and in the gold mines.
I should now like to direct the minister's attention to a news item that appeared in the Ottawa Journal of June 14. It is a Canadian Press dispatch from London. The heading is "Canada Recruits Miners Overseas" and it reads as follows:
William Ramsay, personnel manager of the Canadian metal mining association, left today on a 10-day tour of Denmark, Sweden and Finland to recruit hard-rock miners for Canada.
He has been holding meetings in Britain in recent weeks, interviewing applicants who want to emigrate to Canada to work underground mining gold, silver, uranium and copper in most Canadian provinces from Ontario to the west coast.
"Altogether, 1,206 men have expressed interest in the idea", said Ramsay. "They still have to pass a medical examination, and some, I expect, will drop out."
Most of the meetings were arranged through the Canadian immigration service in Britain.

Supply-Labour
Ramsay, on loan to the mining association from his national employment service job at Kirkland Lake, Ontario, wants husky men between 19 and 35 years of age. He has had pamphlets printed in several languages offering wages-
This is in the mining industry, as miners.
-from a minimum of $1.05 to $1.53 an hour. Some jobs offer an additional production bonus.
"Wages are the same as paid in the locality in which you are working", the pamphlet says.
Now, Mr. Chairman, if that statement is correct and the men are being recruited for work in the mines of Canada at $1.05 per hour, they are being brought to this country under false pretences. They are being offered wages below even the lowest wages paid in the gold mines at the present time. I find that in the Kirkland Lake area out of eight mines, indicating the situation in gold mines as against base metal mines, only one mine is organized in a really effective fashion. There are two that have some form of association which the miners' unions term company unions and three have a recognized union but it is in a very weak condition. There are two that have no union organizations of any kind. I understand that situation prevails in the gold mining industry because many workers are apparently of the opinion that owing to present conditions in that industry they will have little opportunity of improving their working conditions or their wages by supporting a union.
In addition to that, the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, when answering a question I had asked during the debate on emergency gold mining assistance, stated that over a period of 10 years there were only 2,889 persons who had been recruited from abroad to work in the mining industry in Canada. I am quite sure the minister gave me what are technically the correct figures. However, the minister's figures do not tell the whole story. I know from personal experience and from complaints raised by miners in my own constituency that many of these people come to Canada under some other pretext. I know that some come to Canada who are supposed to work on a farm for two years, but it is very natural and very human that when they find the high rate of wages being paid in the mining industry they leave the poor farmer in the lurch. You find them in the mines within six months. We have had a good many cases of that sort. A good many of the people who have come over from Europe, supposedly to work at other employment, have entered the mining industry in the period mentioned by the minister. I do not think his figures represent a true picture in any sense of the word.
I am told by leaders of unions in the mining industry, that is types of leaders who are

recognized by labour as qualified and proper trade unionists, that there is no shortage of miners in the base metal mining industry. I have had that statement made very definitely. They all admit a shortage of miners in the gold mining industry, which I can well understand. It is the result of the basic wage rate as compared to base metal mining, and the result of the working conditions and so on. I have received a good number of complaints from the miners working in my constituency who say that these immigrants who are brought to Canada, as they will be possibly under false pretences in many cases and without a firm knowledge of the mining industry, are a hazard to the miners concerned for two reasons. I have had them tell me that men should not be in the mine who cannot speak the English language sufficiently to be understood by other men.
The second reason is their lack of experience. I know of one case in my own district where miners who have been working in the industry for a good many years had some trouble with the management and refused to go into the mine until some men were removed from the labour force. It was not that they had anything against those men personally. I do not blame these people for trying to improve their conditions. In this case the men did not speak the language and were not able to understand instructions with regard to explosives. They certainly lacked experience as far as hard-rock mining was concerned.
If I remember correctly the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys also said that five gold mines closed last year. I wonder if the Minister of Labour could assure the house that those men who lost employment because of the closing of those mines will find employment in other mines. I am particularly thinking of those who are over age and are not normally employed because of pension plans and things of that sort.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I have briefly dealt with this question again because I think it is one that demands a thorough investigation by the minister to get the facts. While we in this group believe that Canada requires immigrants, we believe in planned immigration. We do not believe in immigration that displaces long-time Canadian workers and Canadian citizens. Let the immigration that is carried on be conducted on a different basis from that on which, according to the news item, information is given to these people who are being recruited in Europe. I do hope the minister gives this matter very close consideration and makes certain the conditions complained of by the miners do not continue to exist.

speechtext:
I wonder if any other hon. member who is thinking of speaking this afternoon would forgive me if I took advantage of the time between now and five o'clock to answer some of the questions, because it may be some few days before my estimates are considered again. I should like to make some comments on some of the things that have been said today.
First of all the hon. member for Hamilton West, as well as other members, gave wholehearted support to our research plans so that we may be in a position to have more knowledge of our professional and technical working force. She referred to the United Kingdom plan with which I had made myself familiar and which I admire very much. Of course she would be the first to agree that you can do things under a unitary system such as the United Kingdom has in this field of education that we cannot do here. I do hate to hark back, but I must say that this whole field of training and education is within the provincial jurisdiction. Having pointed that out, however, I do agree with practically all that has been said, that it is the duty of the government and the duty of the Minister of Labour and his agencies to do everything in their power to forward the effort.
The hon. member for Hamilton West stressed the importance of the decentralization of authority in those agencies coming under the Minister of Labour in order that they may be prepared for an emergency.

maintopic: NEW SUPPLY OF PROFESSIONAL PERSONNEL, CANADA, 1946 TO 1955
speechtext: But only in time of emergency.

maintopic: NEW SUPPLY OF PROFESSIONAL PERSONNEL, CANADA, 1946 TO 1955
speechtext: I agree with her up to a certain point. I do agree that a maximum of advance planning for emergency should be done and that it should encompass those agencies. It should, of course, be co-ordinated with all the other departments of government concerned. This is being done and will continue to be done and kept up to date. On the other hand, I cannot agree with her that agencies such as the unemployment insurance commission and the national employment service, in a time of peace such as we now have, should be on a semi-mobilized basis, whereby a Canadian worker who takes advantage of that service may have the feeling that he may be subject to certain compulsions-

speechtext:
If the minister will permit, I had no such thought in mind. It was merely a matter of making the facilities of the office and its officers available in an emergency, without having regard for the authority which they might not be able to contact. It had nothing to do with any time except a period of emergency.

maintopic: NEW SUPPLY OF PROFESSIONAL PERSONNEL, CANADA, 1946 TO 1955
speechtext:
If these officials were to be available in such emergencies it would have to be after the appropriate legislation for that emergency had been passed by parliament. I can assure my hon. friend that, so far as the planning stage is concerned, that has received attention.
The Leader of the Opposition, the hon. member for Hamilton West and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred to the importance of the revision of the labour code. I have a notion, however, that the revision or the plan leading toward a revision suggested by the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Hamilton West might be somewhat different from that envisaged by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
I believe it is important for us to keep the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act up to date. I do not believe it has all the disadvantages that have been suggested to us today. In saying that I do not want to appear smug or to indicate that we are not giving it a great deal of thought and study. We have been doing that, and I stated in this house last year, when the railway unions were considering the matter of what should be done in their field, that we would be glad to co-operate with them in studying plans for the future. As we stand now, we shall continue to keep this matter under consideration and, when the appropriate time comes, to take action on it.
I agree with the hon. member for Hamilton West that we cannot take approximately 1J million union members lightly. In these postwar years they have displayed evidences of responsibility in their attitude toward conciliation procedure, toward disputes and toward the whole community, which is something that augurs well for the future of labour unionism in Canada in the new larger combined congress.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South said some good things about winter employment and trying to level off the ups and downs of seasonal variation. We did make some good progress last winter. I am not saying that all the improvement was due to the plans that were carried out by a great many people to improve seasonal employment. A good deal of it was due to the fact that there was more work available; but the high peak of unemployment that cropped up in the middle of last winter was not nearly as high as it has been in previous years. As far as my department and the unemployment insurance commission are concerned, they are going to co-operate even more aggressively against unemployment next winter.

Supply-Labour
My hon. friend said-I took down his words -"that the shortage of scientists was greatly overworked". Some other hon. members took exception to that. He may be interested to learn that yesterday or the day before the president of the Du Pont Company of Canada, speaking in Montreal, said almost the same thing. He said, "Grossly overemphasized". That may be so in his particular industry. However, I do not think we can overlook the fact that we do need more professional and skilled personnel, because it is not only the requirements of the industries that are well established and well on the way that we have to think of. We ought to have more of that kind of people to help initiate new industries and new efforts.
On the subject of the movement of workers, the hon. member for Cape Breton South said we were discriminating; that there was a difference, for instance, between the treatment those workers from Cape Breton who are going out to help in the woods industry in British Columbia and the workers who are coming in under the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. There is not as much difference as he indicated. The arrangement with those going west was that we, the Department of Labour, should pay their expenses out or issue them with warrants and in due course the company should refund all the money to the government. The arrangement with the Department of Citizenship and Immigration is much the same, in that they pay the expenses and the new Canadian repays the money.
He spoke of the controversy between those who sponsor the trade school and those who favour the vocational high school. I think we could discuss that for quite a long time, probably with a good deal of usefulness. Certainly in his opinion the mature worker going to a trade school with nothing else on his or her mind than learning a skill is more effective than a teen-ager high school student between grades 10 and 11 who takes a course at the high school and goes down to the basement and learns some manual skills on the machines and on the lathes. The theory there is, of course, that these young people, having obtained a smattering of some skill, when they go out to work and do not go on to university, are better able to enter into the production force of the country. I want to thank him for his kind words regarding the women's bureau and its director. As a matter of fact she happened to be in the gallery at the time he spoke, and I was glad she was able to hear him.
The hon. member for Macleod referred to teamwork in industry and the importance of encouraging it. I thoroughly agree with him,

but I was rather surprised at his pessimism this morning. A member coming from that very rich province of Alberta, he used the word "depression" many times and he used such expressions as "dog eat dog" in industry. In my short period as Minister of Labour since 1950 I have not observed very much of dog eating dog. I believe that during the years since the war there has developed a very high level of responsibility on the part of those who are bargaining and arranging the settlement of disputes, and it is a responsibility not only to those whom they directly represent but to the community as a whole.
The hon. member for York Centre also referred to student aid and the importance of money for training. He said that he was more in favour of providing money for the training of young people in industrial skills than for military training of the old-fashioned type. In that I heartily agree with him.
The hon. member for Broadview criticized the rehabilitation program under the co-ordination arrangements with the provinces, with various departments of government and with the voluntary agencies. He referred to the fact that in the United States last year, through their program which is a great one -I will grant that-they had been able to place some 200,000 handicapped persons in employment. That is a great achievement. In Canada last year we were able to place some 19,773 handicapped persons in industry. We usually multiply our population by 10 and get something approaching the population of the United States. We have had those who were unable to work and could not be placed. Last year over 1,000 were rehabilitated. The first 472 cases originated in the provinces of Alberta, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. These 472 cases and the 228 dependents had been maintained by their families in institutions or by public assistance at an annual cost of some $203,000. In their first year of employment they earned collectively almost $1 million. I admit immediately that the plan under way is a co-operative one that must move reasonably slowly; but in conjunction with my colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare I can report to the committee that good progress is being made.
The hon. member for Vancouver South, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Kootenay West referred to the unfilled mission of our late friend Jack MacDougall. Jack MacDougall, along with Mr. O'Neill who was here some weeks ago representing the superannuated C.P.R. employees, was constant in his efforts to have something done for these men, as were we all. I think most hon. members

know that at that time it was possible for Mr. O'Neill to go to Montreal to see the top echelon of the Canadian Pacific management. I know he made a great impression upon them but unfortunately the success he hoped for was not achieved. I pledge to those who have spoken any assistance I can give to achieve the objectives they have in mind.
The hon. member for Lanark again brought forward the matter of taxation on scholarships. I agree with what he said and I shall discuss this matter with my colleague the Minister of Finance. He spoke also on behalf of older workers between 45 and 65 years of age. We are doing something there. It is not perfect or spectacular, but good solid progress is being made.
I was inspired by the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who made me feel the importance of my role. As he pointed out, it is a great thing to be Minister of Labour for Canada, and I agree heartily that it is a great privilege to serve C nada in this capacity even for a short time. While the speed may not be as fast as he would want it to be, in the past we have made some real progress in carrying out the desires of organized labour and the thoughtful recommendations which they have made at their conventions. I listened to what was said in Toronto and at the C.L.C. convention and I read carefully the speeches and the resolutions. Then each year the government meets with the executive bodies of the labour organizations-this year it will be three instead of four-when we are given details of the projects which they consider to be of utmost importance. In recent years quite a large proportion of those that have been stressed have been carried into effect. I have noted the other points made by the hon. member.
The Leader of the Opposition referred to the importance of reviewing the labour code. I dealt with this when I was replying to the hon. member for Hamilton West. Reference was made also to the national advisory council on manpower. That body was appointed in 1950 at the approach of the emergency in Korea, and it did most useful work in the years following. I outlined that work in the statement I made earlier. The council is still in being and it is my intention to utilize it when we are in possession of more statistics and facts.
