Mr. Speaker, I think the sponsor of the bill would like to move it forward, and on May 11, when this bill was last discussed in the house, I had just about completed my remarks at six o'clock. However, I find that just before I stopped talking I made a statement which was wrong and which I should like to correct now. At that time I was making a summary of the various provincial laws related to vacations with pay. I had said that two weeks' vacation with pay after one year of employment is a standard at the present time in effect in only one province. When I said that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked, "Which one", and in reply I said in error, "British Columbia."
The fact is that such a law has been in force in Saskatchewan for several years. In British Columbia a similar law had been passed but had not been proclaimed at that time, and I believe it will not be proclaimed until two weeks from now, on the 1st of July.
In my remarks at that time I made the point that I felt that within the highly organized industries which come under federal jurisdiction this matter should be left, as my hon. friend said this afternoon in that namby-pamby fashion, to collective bargaining procedures.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: NEW SUPPLY OF PROFESSIONAL PERSONNEL, CANADA, 1946 TO 1955
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF ANNUAL HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext: I said I did not like to see the minister used as a tool of resistance against progressive legislation.

maintopic: NEW SUPPLY OF PROFESSIONAL PERSONNEL, CANADA, 1946 TO 1955
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF ANNUAL HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
I think there is something to be said in this respect. Because of the influence which does attach to federal legislation extending across the country, if we accept two weeks as the proper minimum standard our action may be regarded as pressure on some provinces to provide the same standard whether or not this is a standard which, in the light of their own experience and circumstances, is warranted. The Leader of the Opposition indicated this afternoon that when the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act was passed by parliament it was immediately copied or followed in the province of Ontario.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Applewhaite).]
If, on the other hand, we were to decide that one week after one year of employment is the proper minimum standard, this might be regarded as placing a brake on an upward revision in provinces which may consider it expedient to provide for some increase over one week. We have been influenced in our own thinking up to this point by the fact that without legislation in the federal field, more favourable vacation with pay plans are being adopted year by year, by the fact that the trend toward annual paid vacations has developed in the United States without either state or federal legislation, and by the experience in the United Kingdom where legislation providing for paid vacations is confined to certain industries subject to the wages councils act which are, generally speaking, the industries in which the workers are to a large extent unorganized and which have no counterpart in our federal field.
I should like to call to the attention of hon. members the schedules which you, sir, permitted me to include in my remarks on May 11. Those figures indicate that workers in the federal field are making pretty rapid progress in getting vacations with pay, which is the object of the bill.
In view of the considerations I have mentioned, I am not prepared to support the bill at this time.
Mr. Gordon Churchill (Winnipeg South
Centre): Mr. Speaker, I have been looking at the debate that occurred on May 11 on this subject. I find that on that occasion the sponsor of the bill introduced it, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) spoke, and the debate has not been resumed until now. The general principle of the bill is one that I should like to support, as was done by the member for Hamilton West. If we get, as we should, into the committee stage on this bill we can examine the details carefully and see what changes might be considered necessary, but at this stage of the debate the actual sections of the bill have to be left to one side.
I noticed that in his speech on this subject on May 11 the minister dealt with the problem of legislation and collective bargaining. In other words, he suggested and repeated today that matters such as vacations with pay might better be left to collective bargaining than be introduced by way of legislation. That is a standard argument when measures such as this are brought forward, and there is room for disagreement as to how much should be left to collective bargaining and how much should be enacted by parliament.
However, in this particular instance the idea of vacations with pay has become an

accepted condition of life fairly well across Canada. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the sponsor of the bill, pointed out that British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec all have legislation on this subject, and that New Brunswick has legislation on vacations with pay with a limited application. Hence when you look at the broad picture of Canada you find that 90 per cent, if not more, of the population has accepted the idea of legislation with regard to vacations with pay. I think that fact must be taken into account as an indication that public opinion is in favour -to the extent of 90 per cent of the population-of legislation rather than, as the minister suggests, leaving the matter to collective bargaining.
Then the hon. member for Hamilton West pointed out on May 11-and these are her words as reported in Hansard at page 3834- as follows:
. . . the virtue in the legislation is that it covers all workers, whether or not they are members of unions or negotiating groups. The main argument against leaving arrangements of this sort to negotiating bodies is that those workers who are not unionized are left out and do not enjoy the privileges which may be extended to those who belong to unions.
The minister has indicated that the 400,000 persons who come under federal jurisdiction in labour matters are highly unionized and to that extent, in his opinion, they are looked after in this regard. But I think there is great weight to the argument of the hon. member for Hamilton West when she says that those who are not in the unions and have not the advantage of collective bargaining should receive some consideration, and that this can be done through legislation.
I examined carefully the table which the minister filed on May 11. I checked that table with his statement as he was relating the facts in the table to the course of the argument. As his argument is set out in Hansard, the impression tends to be left that between 6 per cent and 7 per cent of the people under federal jurisdiction are not looked after in so far as vacations with pay are concerned. That happens to be set out in a paragraph by itself and naturally stands out, but it is a bit misleading when you look carefully at the table, because the table shows that over 50 per cent of the employees under federal jurisdiction do not get vacations with pay in the period of one or two years. They must wait for three years, five years or more than five years or else they do not get it at all.
Just recently the minister said that these workers were making-and these were his words-pretty rapid progress in achieving this desirable result of vacations with pay. I think
Industrial Relations
they are not making progress at all, or at least it is very slow progress when you look at that table and see that some of them must wait for five years before they become eligible for a vacation with pay.
Another argument advanced by the minister was that legislation authorizing, for example, one week's vacation with pay after a year's service might tend to put a brake on legislation in the various provinces or collective bargaining looking toward a greater period of vacation than now applies, and that federal legislation authorizing one week's vacation with pay after one year's service might tend to slow down some of these other proposals that are coming forward.
That argument deserves consideration, but I wonder whether it really is a brake on progress. Maybe on the other hand you could say-and I think you can say it with justification-that the general approval given by legislation is helpful to those who are wondering about what they should do with regard to vacations with pay; and if it is established by legislation that it is an accepted, normal practice, then those who are negotiating for better conditions with regard to this problem receive assistance. I therefore do not attach too much weight to the minister's argument with regard to the brake being applied by reason of legislation in this field.
I think this bill should be given second reading and be subjected to the scrutiny of the committee rather than be thrown out at this stage. It is the first time that a bill, in the detailed form required, has been brought before parliament. In other years the subject has been discussed by way of resolution, but on this occasion it has been formalized and the bill is now available for members to look at very closely. Consequently I think it should advance beyond this stage so it can be examined with great care in committee, where there is more opportunity for questions and answers to be exchanged and, of course, for amendments to be brought forward.
I think the general principle is sound, namely that there should be vacations with pay. That principle has been developed over a great many years. As the minister pointed out this afternoon, in the United States of America and in the United Kingdom the idea has been adopted. It is immaterial, for the purpose of what I am saying at the moment, whether it has been done by collective bargaining or by legislation. In these modern industrial states such as ours and the two I have mentioned it has become almost universal practice to provide vacations with pay.
The purpose behind that practice is sound. It is basically for health reasons. If the health of the population is sustained, the industrial

speechtext:
Industrial Relations
strength of the nation is greater. In view of the fact that this practice has become accepted in this way over such a large area of Canada and in other progressive states, I think the time has come for parliament to consider this matter and, as the Leader of the Opposition suggested this afternoon, to accept the suggestion from the opposition side of the house. There is no harm in the government accepting good suggestions that come with such frequency from this side of the chamber, and this happens to be one of them.
I think the federal government should not be lagging in progressive matters. Sometimes the federal government, in moving forward ahead of some of the provinces, shows the way and gives the provinces a lead as to what might be done. In this particular instance I think federal legislation would be helpful to the provinces which perhaps have not yet seriously considered this question of vacations with pay. I see no objection to the parliament of Canada giving a lead to the provinces generally. It is done in other matters and I do not see why it cannot be done in this field. For these and other reasons that I might bring forward, I am prepared to support this bill.

maintopic: NEW SUPPLY OF PROFESSIONAL PERSONNEL, CANADA, 1946 TO 1955
speechtext:
I for
one, in rising to support the bill that is before the house, would like to see a bill of this nature go before the industrial relations committee. I am quite sure, though I cannot recall him mentioning it, that the mover of the bill would have no objection to that course being followed. The hon. member informs me he so stated when he opened the discussion on second reading.
When this matter was discussed on May 11 the Minister of Labour set out in some detail the position he intended to take, which position he again summarized for the house this afternoon. I must say that I regret he was not sufficiently moved by the exhortation made earlier this afternoon by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that he might act a little more in the role of a visionary or a prophet by putting forward to his colleagues advances in labour and social legislation. Perhaps he does more of that behind the scenes than he does on the floor of the house. He may have noticed that we on this side were encouraged by his fairly forthright statement in respect to wages that are paid in the gold mining industry.
I would say that had he seen fit this afternoon to rise and state that he would be prepared to support the principle of this bill and have it go to the industrial relations committee for study, he would have received an even more vociferous round of applause from some of us over on this side of the house.
I must say that having looked over some of the remarks made on May 11 I find it difficult to call the line of reasoning which he sets forth there as "liberal". Rather it is much more the line of argument that has already been described, that this is a matter that should be left to be decided by the process of collective bargaining. I am going to read briefly from the minister's remarks, just to refresh the minds of hon. members. This is found on page 3838 of Hansard for May 11, 1956:
Where working conditions for a large proportion of employees in any jurisdiction are already established by collective bargaining, it could very well be that standardization through legislation is not desirable. When working conditions are left to collective bargaining there is the ability to inject into them a flexibility in determining standards which is lacking when any government introduces minimum standards. In some instances an increase in wages or salaries or an improvement in some one or more fringe benefits may be more acceptable to the employees than a longer paid vacation leave.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that in relation to the subject matter of this bill, I found the latter part of the minister's argument to be rather specious. In the first instance the statistics he gave us on that occasion indicate that only 46-7 per cent of the employees who come under the jurisdiction of federal legislation in the field of labour now enjoy, through the collective bargaining process, the proposal that this bill makes. In my opinion he entirely disregards the fact that the people who do not enjoy that position, by and large, are those who certainly have not the bargaining power to secure the other fringe benefit to which he referred in the latter part of his statement.
I think the truth of what I am suggesting is demonstrated by the fact that the organized labour congress and the strongly organized unions, who have holiday provisions as good as or better than those the bill would provide, are the strongest advocates of the adoption of suitable minimum legislation in the field of annual holidays, as they are in other fields of labour legislation. They do not need it, but they recognize that there are large elements of the working force of this country who are not in a position to organize as effectively as they have organized and to win the conditions which they enjoy through collective bargaining.
Certainly I have never, at the large number of trade union conventions of various kinds which I have attended, heard the complaint that the provision of minimum standards by legislation reduced the flexibility of the trade union movement in its bargaining position. I do not know from what source I have heard that argument except
TMr. Churchill.]

from the conservative-minded Minister of Labour, or should I say a Minister of Labour expressing a rather conservative attitude on behalf of the government. I feel that even now, in spite of what the Minister of Labour has already stated, he might consider the suggestion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre that this bill be allowed to proceed past second reading and go to the standing committee on industrial relations for detailed study.
At this point I should like to appeal to some of my colleagues on the other side of the house who come from British Columbia to express their personal views on this subject matter. I remember being rather delighted on one occasion, I am not sure whether it was last session or the session before, when a bill affecting the rights of labour was introduced by my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and all the British Columbia members on the other side of the house rose in support of that bill. I am quite sure they could have a great leavening effect upon the conservative position which the minister has taken if they would get up and extol the virtues of the legislative provisions for annual holidays which we have enjoyed in British Columbia for a good many years. I am sure if they got up they would say this legislation was introduced by a government in which the Liberal party comprised certainly the largest element.
I am sure they would confirm what I have been saying. This matter is so generally accepted in British Columbia at the present time that the provision which was put through the legislature at the last session in Victoria created very little stir. In my opinion it was thrown in at the tag end of the session in Victoria as something of a sop to the labour movement of British Columbia because of the fact that every other demand that organized labour had been making in British Columbia had met a flat refusal by the administration there. Nevertheless I will say that, as far as I am aware, from no political quarter in British Columbia was any objection whatsoever raised to the fact that next year our holidays with pay act will include this provision of two weeks instead of one week of annual holidays with pay.
I do not think there is a great deal more that I can usefully add to the discussion that has taken place, Mr. Speaker, except perhaps to say in closing that to my mind this is one of the subjects which is almost self-evident as a suitable field for legislation in this era in which we live. Because of the pace of our modern industrial society it is becoming almost universally recognized in the minds of 67509-324
Industrial Relations
all people with any liberality in their minds at all that an annual holiday from the hectic pace of the society in which we live is as essential to the maintenance of a decent standard of living as food and clothing.
Apart from anything else, if we are going to take corrective measures to reduce the number of cases of people who break down under the strain of our society and who have to find protection, at heavy public expense in some instances, in various sorts of institutions which society provides, we have a responsibility to the people of Canada to reduce the incidence of that sort of thing by providing by legislation that every working person in this country will have the opportunity of at least one period of annual respite from his labours.

maintopic: NEW SUPPLY OF PROFESSIONAL PERSONNEL, CANADA, 1946 TO 1955
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the eloquent appeal of the hon. member for Comox-Albemi that some of us on this side express our opinions on this matter, perhaps I shall do some thinking out loud for a change and just say that sometimes some of us on this side find ourselves on the spot. I for one would certainly not speak or vote against any subject on which the government had taken a firm and final position, and certainly not on any matter of want of confidence. But, as the hon. member has pointed out, on these private bills we do enjoy a very wide measure of discretion.
I think there has been every encouragement from all ministers on this side, from the Prime Minister down, to private members to express their personal opinions. I believe hon. members know that on some occasions, even when the hon. member for Hamilton West was introducing a bill which I did not think was a particularly good bill, we have followed that line. I thought the hon. member for Hamilton West was trying to do what was the right thing, but I did not think her bill was a particularly good one; yet I both spoke for it and voted for it because I thought it was a step in the right direction.
I frankly confess I am not sure whether it is a good thing to try to do by legislation what all hon. members opposite have pointed out is being pretty well done already by the ordinary processes of collective bargaining. The hon. member who has just taken his seat has pointed out that in British Columbia, where we come from, this has no practical bearing at all for, as he has said, we have had for a good many years not only legislation but action as the result of collective bargaining which goes a good deal further than this proposed legislation goes.

Industrial Relations

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: NEW SUPPLY OF PROFESSIONAL PERSONNEL, CANADA, 1946 TO 1955
speechtext: Only with respect to employees under the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature.

maintopic: NEW SUPPLY OF PROFESSIONAL PERSONNEL, CANADA, 1946 TO 1955
speechtext:
Of course, only with respect to employees under provincial legislation. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre knows that they are the overwhelming majority and this would apply simply to a small minority. As the hon. member for Comox-Alberni pointed out, the great labour organizations of Canada, the new amalgamated labour organization which is so powerful and of which we all have such great hopes, and which we think will contribute much to this country, even though their members will not benefit in any great way from the legislation proposed, they have given it their moral support.
Contrary to what my hon. friend has just suggested, I think some of the speeches which were made on May 11 had some pretty good points on the opposite side. It seems to me that some of the speeches at least tended to show that one of the weaknesses of this legislation might be this. We all know that when you pass legislation that legislation tends to set the floor, tends to become the standard. If one effect of the passage of the legislation is to minimize rights which it is said unorganized workers or unprotected workers have already won, then it seems to me that it is a bad thing to have the law.
It might be said that I am thinking out loud. I frankly confess that I would be better pleased if our ministers and our government took a slightly different attitude on some of these welfare proposals that come up from time to time. I will frankly mention things like the check-off, and holidays with pay, and I could mention two or three others. I know very well the general argument is that these things are already being looked after by the collective bargaining process, or by provincial legislation, and therefore there is no particular need for us to have federal action along that line. But the federal government has a responsibility to help to set the pace in these things from time to time, and even its moral effect can be important in that regard.
As the hon. member for Comox-Alberni pointed out, during the long life of the Liberal regime in British Columbia, in which we had a very enlightened minister of labour even in the days when it became a coalition government, the attitude we took was quite different from the attitude that is sometimes expressed in this house. Our attitude was this. We felt that harmonious relations between employers and employees were in the interest of the whole country. We know

that in most cases disputes between the two branches of industry centre on wages and hours. We know there is another category of dispute which concerns what we might call fringe benefits. I think this is one of the things that would be included in that category. We also know that there is one other great category of labour disputes. In fact some of the most damaging labour disputes we have ever had in Canada were in a different category altogether; that is the category of whether unions have the right to organize and be recognized legally after they have signed up 51 per cent of the workers.
I know there are many hon. members who have been in this house a lot longer than I, but I do not think there are many who remember more of the history of the improvement in general labour laws and labour relations in this country than I. I am sometimes amazed and greatly encouraged by the great improvement which has occurred even in my lifetime. I remember that when I first went to British Columbia about 20 years ago I went to a town, the name of which I shall not mention, to make a speech before the Canadian Club. An organizer for the mine union arrived in the town the same day I did, and within half an hour the brakes had been taken off his car and the car was allowed to run down a hill to be smashed to bits and pieces. At that time the whole atmosphere of labour relations in this country was in a most primitive and backward state compared to what it is now.
We know that chiefly as the result of an improved outlook on the part of the public, certainly in British Columbia, a great improvement has taken place. One of the reasons for improvement in that province was the enlightened legislation placed on the statute books by the minister of labour, who believed it was a good thing to take these matters out of the category of what were termed fringe benefits, certainly to take out of the category of controversy the right of a union to organize peaceably and be recognized by the employer and by the law if it could get 51 per cent of the workers.
We know that as a result of legislation introduced in British Columbia by a Liberal minister of labour that province set the pace for the entire Dominion of Canada. The labour laws which went into effect officially right across the country and which gave to the unions of this country the right to organize in peace and be recognized under the law dated from that enlightened legislation passed in British Columbia.
It seems to me that the attitude adopted by the British Columbia minister of labour has some slight bearing on this particular

case today. He thought it was better to grant these things by law than to have them fought over in the ordinary process of collective bargaining. He thought it was better to take these things entirely out of the realm of annual dispute and annual negotiation which would take place between the employer and the employee.
There is one other consideration that appeals to me in connection with this particular bill. Even though it does not do anything to protect those who are protected already, that is those who have the protection of a powerful trade union, it seems to me that the proposal would go a long way toward granting justice to the classes in the community which need protection the most, that is the young girl, the young man or perhaps the new immigrant who has come to this country and knows nothing about the way we operate, knows nothing about our trade unions and so on. This would give a certain protection by law to those people who do not have the support of powerful trade unions.
There is a negative side to this bill, in that it would tend to lower the general level of holidays to be granted, just as a floor price under butter tends to fix the price at that

level. If a floor under holidays were set by the government, that would tend to become the general level. I think that has been true in connection with minimum wages covering the lower classes of workers. My thinking at this time is that on balance I do not see how I could vote against this legislation. I would certainly be in favour of voting for the legislation at least to the extent of sending it to the committee on industrial relations, where it could be examined.
On motion of Mr. Philpott the debate was adjourned.
